docs.title: TBL Documentation
docs.text:
Docs for building Telegram bots on TeleBotHost with TBL (Tele Bot Language).

TeleBotHost runs your bot in the cloud. TBL is the code you write in the command editor — JavaScript-shaped syntax, built-in Telegram tools, no server to manage.

docs.title: New here?
docs.text:
1. Getting Started — account, BotFather token, launch your bot
  2. Tutorials — six short lessons from /start to wildcard handlers
  3. What is TBL? — how commands run and why the model looks the way it does

Once /start works, read Bot vs Api. It saves a lot of confusion later.

docs.title: Reference sections
docs.text:
Instances — the objects you call in command logic:

  • Bot — flow, storage, simple sends
  • Api — full Telegram Bot API access
  • HTTP — outbound requests to external services
  • User / Global — per-user and bot-wide data
  • msg — reply, edit, delete on the current message
  • Webhooks / Webapps — HTTP endpoints tied to commands
  • res — JSON, HTML, redirects from webhook/Webapp commands

Global Variables — user, chat, update, message, and the rest of the context available while a command runs.

Modules and Libraries — lodash, jwt, date helpers, Telegram utilities, and other preloaded tools.

docs.title: What is TBL?
docs.text:
TBL (Tele Bot Language) is what you write inside TeleBotHost to make a bot do things.

It's not a general-purpose language for building websites or CLI tools. It's for Telegram bots — receiving updates, sending replies, storing user data, calling external APIs when you need to. TeleBotHost handles hosting; TBL handles bot behavior.

New to the platform? Getting Started. Want to write code? Learning TBL.

docs.title: Commands, not event loops
docs.text:
Most Node bot frameworks look like this: register listeners, keep a process alive, hope nothing leaks. TBL flips that.

Telegram sends an update. TBL finds the matching command and runs it. The command finishes. Nothing stays running in the background waiting for the next message — the next update starts a fresh execution.

That makes behavior easier to reason about. One update, one command, one path through the code.

docs.title: Short-lived executions
docs.text:
Each run is sandboxed and time-bounded. Your command does its work — send messages, read storage, call HTTP — and exits. Under load, many users can trigger commands at once without one long-running script getting tangled.

You won't find background timers or daemons in TBL by design. If something should happen "later," it's because a new update arrived or you chained work through on_run / another command.

docs.title: Async when it helps
docs.text: Some calls take time — Telegram's API, an external HTTP request. TBL supports await where you need the result before continuing. It doesn't push async everywhere; only where waiting actually matters.

docs.title: Why the limits exist
docs.text:
TBL deliberately isn't Node.js. You can't install arbitrary npm packages or open raw sockets. That frustrates people who want a full server — and protects everyone else from accidental infinite loops, runaway memory, or bots that become impossible to debug.

The tradeoff: less flexibility, faster path to a working bot.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide walks you through creating and running your first Telegram bot on TeleBotHost.

docs.title: 1. Open TeleBotHost
docs.text: Go to the TeleBotHost console.

docs.title: 2. Log In or Sign Up

  • Create a new account if you are new

After logging in, you will see the dashboard.

docs.title: 3. Create a Telegram Bot
docs.text:
1. Open Telegram
  2. Search for @BotFather
  3. Send /newbot
  4. Set a bot name and username
  5. Copy the bot token provided

docs.title: 4. Add the Bot on TeleBotHost
docs.text:
1. Open the TeleBotHost dashboard
  2. Click Add Bot
  3. Paste your bot token
  4. Click Create

Your bot will appear in the bot list.

docs.text:
Click your bot in the dashboard to open its management panel.

From here you can:

  • Add and edit commands
  • Write TBL code
  • Start or stop the bot

docs.text:
Click Launch Bot to start your bot.

Your bot is now online and ready to respond on Telegram.

  2. Add a command such as /start
  3. Save the command

Test it by sending /start to your bot on Telegram.

docs.title: Learning TBL
docs.text:
TBL looks like JavaScript because it mostly is — same syntax for variables, if, loops, objects. What's different is what's already there: Bot, Api, user, chat, no npm install, no Express server.

You write logic inside commands. Telegram sends an update, TBL picks a command, your code runs, execution ends. That's the whole lifecycle.

docs.title: Sync by default
docs.text:
Lines run in order. Most Bot and Api calls work that way out of the box.

When you need a response before continuing — grab a message id, check whether send succeeded — add await:

let sent = await Api.sendMessage({ text: "One moment..." })
await sent.editText("Ready.")

Don't sprinkle await on calls where you ignore the result.

docs.title: Your first line of code
docs.text:
Bot.sendMessage("Hello from TBL.");

Drop that in a command's logic field, trigger the command on Telegram, you get a reply. Everything else builds from there.

docs.title: res.render() In-Depth
docs.text:
The res.render() method is used to render another command or template as an HTTP response.

It automatically detects the response content type, renders templates when needed, and exposes useful context data to the rendered command.

This makes it ideal for building web pages, APIs, dashboards, and webapps using TBL.

For all res methods, see the Response (res) overview. For a shorter template guide, see Template Rendering.

docs.title: Automatic Content Type Detection
docs.text:
res.render() automatically sets the correct Content-Type based on the file extension.

Examples:

res.render("page.html")        // Content-Type: text/html
res.render("data.json")        // Content-Type: application/json
res.render("script.js")        // Content-Type: application/javascript
res.render("style.css")        // Content-Type: text/css
res.render("api.xml")          // Content-Type: application/xml
res.render("plain-text")       // Content-Type: text/plain

No manual headers are required.

docs.title: Data Passing and Template Context
docs.text:
You can pass data to res.render() using the second argument.

Example webapp URL:

/webapp/showProfile?section=settings&view=compact

Example render call:

res.render("profile-template.html", {
  data: {
    user: user,
    profile: userProfile,
    preferences: userPrefs
  }
})

docs.title: Available Data Inside the Rendered Template
docs.text:
Inside profile-template.html, you can access:

  • user – current user object (user-based webhook only)
  • profile – custom data passed via data
  • preferences – custom data passed via data
  • params – URL query parameters { section: "settings", view: "compact" }
  • All global TBL variables (Api, Bot, msg, request, etc.)

Example usage inside template:

<h1>Welcome <%= user.first_name %></h1>
<p>Profile: <%= profile %></p>

docs.title: Example 1: JSON API Endpoint
docs.text:
This example returns structured JSON data.

let userData = {
  id: user.id,
  name: user.first_name,
  premium: user.premium || false,
  join_date: user.join_date
}

res.status(200)
   .set("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", "*")
   .json({
     status: "success",
     data: userData,
     timestamp: Date.now()
   })

Note

The user object is available only in user-based webhooks.

docs.title: Example 2: Render an HTML Page
docs.text:
res.render("dashboard.html", {
  data: {
    stats: statsData,
    user: user
  }
})

This renders an HTML page with EJS support.

docs.title: Example 3: Render JSON via Template
docs.text:
res.render("api-response.json", {
  data: {
    ok: true,
    result: resultData
  }
})

Content type is automatically set to application/json.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• res.render() ends execution immediately
  • Content type is detected automatically
  • EJS rendering works for HTML and text
  • params always contains query parameters
  • User data is available only in user-based webhooks

Tip

Use res.render() to keep API logic and presentation cleanly separated.

docs.title: Response Object (res)
docs.text:
The res instance sends custom HTTP responses from webhook and Webapp commands.

It lets your bot behave like an HTTP API or web endpoint. You can return JSON, HTML, XML, plain text, redirects, and rendered templates (EJS).

Once a response is sent with res, command execution ends.

Availability

The res instance is available in webhook commands and Webapp commands — not in normal Telegram message commands.

docs.title: set(key, value)
docs.text:
Sets HTTP headers on the response.

res.set("Content-Type", "application/json")
   .set("X-Custom-Header", "my-value")

Headers can be chained.

docs.title: status(code)
docs.text:
Sets the HTTP response status code.

res.status(200)
res.status(404)
res.status(500)

You can chain this with other methods.

docs.title: send(body)
docs.text:
Sends a response with any content type.

res.send("Hello World")
res.send({ message: "Success", data: { id: 1 } })
res.status(201).send("Resource created")

The content type is auto-detected.

docs.title: json(obj)
docs.text:
Sends a JSON response with application/json content type.

res.json({
  status: "success",
  user: user.name,
  data: processedData
})

This is the most common method for API-style responses.

docs.title: html(content)
docs.text:
Sends an HTML response.

If EJS tags are detected, the content is automatically rendered.

res.html("<h1>Welcome</h1><p>Hello World</p>")

With EJS rendering:

res.html(`
  <h1>Welcome <%= user.first_name %></h1>
  <p>Your ID: <%= user.id %></p>
  <% if (user.premium) { %>
    <div class='premium'>Premium User</div>
  <% } %>
`)

docs.title: xml(content)
docs.text:
Sends an XML response with application/xml content type.

res.xml('<?xml version="1.0"?><response><status>success</status></response>')

docs.title: text(content)
docs.text:
Sends a plain text response.

EJS templates are auto-rendered if detected.

res.text("This is plain text")

const textTemplate = "Hello <%= name %>, welcome!"
res.text(textTemplate)

docs.title: redirect(url)
docs.text:
Redirects the request to another URL or command.

res.redirect("https://example.com/success")
res.redirect("/another-command")

Redirect responses are sent immediately.

docs.title: render(commandPath, options)
docs.text:
Renders another command's output as the response.

Content type is detected automatically based on the target.

res.render("user-profile")

With options:

res.render("api-data.json", {
  data: { user: { name: "John", age: 30 } }
})

Rendering an HTML command:

res.render("dashboard.html", {
  data: {
    user: user,
    stats: userStats,
    params: params
  }
})

For advanced res.render() usage, see the res.render() Guide.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Sending a response ends execution
  • Headers, status, and body can be chained
  • EJS rendering works automatically for HTML and text
  • If no response is sent, a default 2xx response is returned
  • The user object in templates is available in user-based webhooks, not in public Webapp URLs

docs.title: The TBL Language
docs.text:
TeleBotHost bots run on TBL — short for Tele Bot Language.

If you've written any JavaScript, the syntax will look familiar: variables, objects, if, functions, await. What's different is the environment. Bot, Api, user, and chat are already there. You don't bootstrap a server or wire up a Telegram library.

docs.title: Not Node, not Python
docs.text:
You can't paste a Express app or a python-telegram-bot script into TeleBotHost and expect it to run. TBL is its own runtime — smaller, sandboxed, built around commands.

That's intentional. The sandbox limits what code can do, which keeps bots stable and makes it harder to accidentally ship something dangerous.

docs.title: What you gain
docs.text:
No VPS. No webhook nginx config. No keeping a process alive on a $5 droplet. You write commands in the dashboard, launch the bot, TeleBotHost runs it.

Telegram integration isn't a dependency you install — it's the platform.

docs.title: A line of TBL
docs.text:
Bot.sendMessage("Hi");

That's a complete interaction pattern in one call. Everything else in the docs builds on moments like that.

docs.title: Read next
docs.text:
• What is TBL? — how commands execute
  • Learning TBL — sync, async, first steps
  • Tutorials — build a bot hands-on

If you come from JavaScript, you'll be productive quickly. If you don't, the tutorials still work — start with Your First Bot and ignore the code until you're ready.

docs.title: Api
docs.text:
Api is how your bot talks to Telegram.

Every method maps to something in the Telegram Bot API — sendMessage, editMessageText, answerCallbackQuery, and hundreds of others. TBL wraps those calls so you don't build HTTP requests or hunt for chat IDs on every line.

Api is already there inside every command. No import, no setup.

Api.sendMessage({ text: "Hey." })

That sends to whoever triggered the command. TBL fills in the chat automatically.

docs.title: When you'd use Api over Bot
docs.text:
Bot is for moving around inside your bot — running another command, storing bot-level data, keeping flows tidy. Api is for when you need Telegram itself: inline buttons, message edits, callback answers, stickers, polls, anything the Bot API exposes.

Rough rule: if you're shaping what the user sees in Telegram, you're probably in Api territory. If you're deciding what your bot does next, look at Bot first. The Bot vs Api guide goes deeper with side-by-side examples.

docs.title: How calls work
docs.text:
Pass a single object with the parameters Telegram expects:

Api.sendPhoto({
  photo: "https://example.com/photo.jpg",
  caption: "Here's the file you asked for.",
  parse_mode: "Markdown"
})

Most methods target the current chat — the conversation where the command fired. Pass chat_id only when you intentionally need a different destination, and only if your bot actually has access there.

Some calls return a response you can use right away:

let sent = await Api.sendMessage({ text: "Processing..." })
await sent.editText("Done.")

Others support on_run, which hands off to another command when Telegram responds. Handy when you want to keep the current command short.

If a method exists in Telegram's docs but not yet as Api.methodName, use Api.call("methodName", { ... }). That keeps you from waiting on platform updates.

docs.title: Error behavior worth knowing
docs.text:
Call a method that doesn't exist — Api.hitMe() — and TBL throws. Your ! error handler catches it.

Send a message to a blocked user or pass a bad parameter, and Telegram returns an error. That usually doesn't crash the command; it shows up in your bot's error logs. Use await and check res.ok when failure would change what you do next. See Tips and Limitations.

docs.title: What's in this section
docs.text:
Page What it covers Sending Messages Text, formatting, basic options Inline Keyboards Buttons under messages, callback data Media and Files Photos, documents, audio, video Editing Messages Change text, captions, keyboards after send Async Requests await and working with responses inline Callbacks on_run and continuing in another command Method Chaining Edit, pin, delete the message you just sent Dynamic Methods Api.call() for anything Telegram adds Tips and Limitations Errors, gotchas, things people miss

Start with Sending Messages if you've never called Api before.

docs.title: Async Requests
docs.text:
Put await in front of an Api call when the next line needs what Telegram sent back.

let me = await Api.getMe()

if (me.ok) {
  Api.sendMessage({ text: "Bot id: " + me.result.id })
}

Execution pauses at the await, the request completes, and me holds the response. Then the command continues.

docs.title: What you get back
docs.text:
Responses follow Telegram's shape: typically ok (boolean) and result (the useful payload). Failed calls set ok to false — check it when the failure would change your logic.

let sent = await Api.sendMessage({ text: "Hello again." })

if (!sent.ok) {
  // user blocked the bot, chat gone, etc.
}

Without that check, the failure only appears in your platform error logs. The command keeps running as if nothing went wrong.

docs.title: Message sends return something useful
docs.text:
When you await Api.sendMessage, the return value is also a chainable object — edit, delete, pin the message you just created. See Method Chaining.

let msg = await Api.sendMessage({ text: "Loading..." })
await msg.editText("Done.")

docs.title: Don't await everything
docs.text:
If you fire a message and don't care about the response, skip await:

Api.sendMessage({ text: "Got it, processing." })
// command continues immediately

Extra awaits add wait time without benefit.

docs.title: Works with dynamic calls too
docs.text:
let chat = await Api.call("getChat", { chat_id: chat.id })

Same rules — check ok, read result.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Callbacks — defer handling to another command with on_run
  • Tips and Limitations — TBL errors vs Telegram errors

docs.title: Callbacks with on_run
docs.text:
Some Api calls finish later. Instead of blocking the whole command with await, you can tell TBL to run another command when Telegram responds.

That's on_run:

Api.getMe({ on_run: "afterGetMe" })

When getMe completes, the afterGetMe command runs automatically. The response lands in options.

docs.title: Why bother?
docs.text:
Splitting work across commands keeps each one readable. The first command starts the Api call. The second handles whatever came back. No nested if-blocks stretching down the page.

You'll see this pattern in bots that call several Telegram methods in sequence but don't want one giant command file.

docs.title: Reading the response
docs.text:
Inside afterGetMe:

if (options.ok) {
  Api.sendMessage({
    text: "Running as @" + options.result.username
  })
} else {
  Api.sendMessage({ text: "Couldn't fetch bot info." })
}

options.ok tells you whether Telegram accepted the call. options.result holds the payload — shape depends on which Api method you used.

TBL passes this automatically. You don't serialize it yourself.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
Command A  →  Api.getMe({ on_run: "B" })  →  Telegram responds  →  Command B runs with options

Command A ends after firing the request. Command B picks up the thread.

docs.title: When to use on_run vs await
docs.text:
await when the next few lines in the same command need the result. Fetch chat info, then immediately send a message based on it — keep it together.

on_run when the follow-up is logically a separate step, or when you want to reuse the same handler command from multiple places.

Both are valid. It's mostly about how you like to organize commands.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• on_run must name a real command in your bot
  • The callback command runs like any other — same globals, same instances
  • Errors in the original call still surface through options; runtime typos still hit your ! handler

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Async Requests — await in one command
  • options variable — full picture of what gets passed

docs.title: Dynamic Methods
docs.text:
Telegram adds API methods regularly. TBL adds wrappers for the common ones, but you shouldn't have to wait for a platform update to use something new in Telegram's docs.

Api.call() forwards any official method by name:

Api.call("getChat", { chat_id: chat.id })

First argument: exact Telegram method name. Second: parameter object, same as the API reference.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Use built-in methods when they exist. Api.sendMessage reads better than Api.call("sendMessage", ...).

Use Api.call when they don't. New Telegram feature, niche method, something not wrapped yet — call it directly.

docs.title: Responses work the same
docs.text:
You can await dynamic calls. You get ok and result. You can pass on_run. Same contract as Api.getChat would have if it were built in.

let res = await Api.call("getChatMember", {
  chat_id: chat.id,
  user_id: user.id
})

docs.title: Parameters are on you
docs.text: TBL doesn't validate dynamic calls against Telegram's schema. Wrong parameter name? Telegram errors. Check the official API docs — parameter names must match exactly.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
If getChat weren't available as Api.getChat:

Api.call("getChat", { chat_id: 4444443444 })

In practice, prefer the built-in wrapper when you see it in the docs. Keep Api.call for the gaps.

docs.title: Editing Messages
docs.text:
Messages don't have to be permanent. Telegram lets bots edit text, captions, and keyboards on messages they sent — and Api exposes all of it.

You'll edit messages constantly in menu-driven bots: swap button labels, replace a status line, remove buttons after the user picks an option.

docs.title: Edit text
docs.text:
Api.editMessageText({
  chat_id: chat.id,
  message_id: message.message_id,
  text: "Updated content.",
  parse_mode: "Markdown"
})

You need the message_id of the message you're changing. In a callback handler that's usually update.callback_query.message.message_id. If you just sent the message yourself, await Api.sendMessage(...) and chain .editText() instead — see Method Chaining.

docs.title: Edit caption on media
docs.text:
Photos and documents use captions, not message text:

Api.editMessageCaption({
  chat_id: chat.id,
  message_id: message.message_id,
  caption: "Revised caption."
})

docs.title: Swap the inline keyboard
docs.text:
Remove buttons after a choice, or replace the whole menu:

Api.editMessageReplyMarkup({
  chat_id: chat.id,
  message_id: message.message_id,
  reply_markup: {
    inline_keyboard: [[{ text: "Done", callback_data: "done" }]]
  }
})

Pass an empty inline_keyboard: [] to strip buttons entirely.

docs.title: Delete instead of edit
docs.text:
Sometimes deletion is cleaner:

Api.deleteMessage({
  chat_id: chat.id,
  message_id: message.message_id
})

Or, if you have the chained response object:

let msg = await Api.sendMessage({ text: "Temporary notice." })
await msg.delete()

docs.title: What you can't edit
docs.text:
Bots can't edit messages they didn't send (with the usual Telegram exceptions around admins and channels). They also can't turn a text message into a photo — edit the text or send new media.

Telegram returns an error if the message is too old or the content is identical to what's already there. Check res.ok when using await.

docs.title: Typical callback flow
docs.text:
1. User taps inline button
  2. Api.answerCallbackQuery(...) — dismiss the spinner
  3. Api.editMessageText(...) — update the same message
  4. Optionally Bot.runCommand(...) — start a new flow

That pattern keeps chats tidy. One message morphs instead of five new ones stacking up.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Full parameter lists live in the Telegram docs:

  • editMessageText
  • editMessageCaption
  • editMessageReplyMarkup
  • deleteMessage

docs.title: Inline Keyboards
docs.text:
Inline buttons sit inside the message bubble — not in the keyboard area at the bottom of the screen. Users tap them; Telegram sends a callback query to your bot; you respond with Api.

Reply keyboards (the Help, About style from the tutorials) are different. Those send plain text. Inline buttons send structured callback data.

docs.title: A minimal keyboard
docs.text:
Api.sendMessage({
  text: "Choose:",
  reply_markup: {
    inline_keyboard: [
      [{ text: "Website", url: "https://telebothost.com" }],
      [{ text: "Help", callback_data: "help" }]
    ]
  }
})

URL buttons open a link. callback_data buttons fire a callback query — you'll handle that in a command triggered by the callback.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Each inner array is a row. Buttons in the same row sit side by side:

reply_markup: {
  inline_keyboard: [
    [{ text: "Yes", callback_data: "yes" }, { text: "No", callback_data: "no" }],
    [{ text: "Cancel", callback_data: "cancel" }]
  ]
}

Two buttons on the first row, one full-width button below.

docs.title: Answering callbacks
docs.text:
When someone taps a callback button, Telegram expects a response — even if it's just "ok, I got it." Without answerCallbackQuery, the client shows a loading spinner on the button.

Api.answerCallbackQuery({
  callback_query_id: update.callback_query.id,
  text: "Saved."
})

The optional text pops a small toast at the top of the chat. Keep it short.

docs.title: Updating the message they tapped
docs.text:
Often you want to change the message instead of sending a new one:

Api.editMessageText({
  chat_id: chat.id,
  message_id: update.callback_query.message.message_id,
  text: "You picked Help. Here's what that means..."
})

Or swap the keyboard while leaving the text alone — editMessageReplyMarkup. Editing Messages walks through both.

docs.title: callback_data limits
docs.text: Telegram caps callback_data at 64 bytes. Don't stash JSON in there. Store an ID or short token, look up the rest in User storage or Bot storage.

docs.title: URL vs callback
docs.text:
Button type User sees Your bot receives url Opens browser / in-app view Nothing callback_data Stays in chat Callback query update

Mix them freely in the same keyboard.

docs.title: Media and Files
docs.text: Text gets you far. Eventually you'll send photos, PDFs, voice notes, or stickers. Api mirrors Telegram's media methods — same object style as sendMessage.

docs.title: Photos
docs.text:
Api.sendPhoto({
  photo: "https://example.com/screenshot.png",
  caption: "Here's what your dashboard looks like."
})

photo accepts a URL, a file_id from a previous upload, or a file reference your bot already has on Telegram's servers. URLs are the quickest way to test; file_id is what you want in production so Telegram doesn't re-fetch the same image every time.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
For PDFs, archives, anything that isn't treated as an inline photo:

Api.sendDocument({
  document: "https://example.com/report.pdf",
  caption: "Monthly report"
})

Users get a download-style attachment.

docs.title: Audio and voice
docs.text:
Api.sendAudio({
  audio: "https://example.com/track.mp3",
  title: "Intro theme"
})

Api.sendVoice({
  voice: "https://example.com/note.ogg"
})

Voice messages show the round player UI. Audio files show as music tracks with metadata.

docs.title: Video
docs.text:
Api.sendVideo({
  video: "https://example.com/demo.mp4",
  caption: "Product walkthrough",
  supports_streaming: true
})

docs.title: Stickers and animations
docs.text:
Stickers use sendSticker. GIF-style clips use sendAnimation. Both take a file_id or upload source the same way as photos.

Check the Telegram Bot API media methods for the full parameter list — dimensions, thumbnails, spoiler flags, and so on all pass through unchanged.

docs.title: Captions and formatting
docs.text: Most media methods accept caption and parse_mode just like messages. Same Markdown rules apply — don't get clever with nested formatting on day one.

docs.title: Sending media as a reply
docs.text:
Add reply_to_message_id if the file should thread under a specific message:

Api.sendDocument({
  document: fileUrl,
  reply_to_message_id: message.message_id
})

docs.title: Bot.sendPhoto vs Api.sendPhoto
docs.text: Bot.sendPhoto("url", "caption") works for quick sends inside bot flows. When you need keyboard markup, spoiler mode, or precise Telegram options, use Api.

docs.title: Chaining after send
docs.text:
let photo = await Api.sendPhoto({ photo: url, caption: "Draft" })
await photo.editCaption("Final version")

See Method Chaining for edit and delete helpers on the returned object.

docs.title: Method Chaining
docs.text:
Send a message with Api, get back an object you can act on immediately — edit it, reply to it, pin it, delete it — without hunting for message_id.

let msg = await Api.sendMessage({ text: "Hello." })

await msg.pin()
await msg.react("👍")
await msg.editText("Updated.")
await msg.reply("Follow-up.")
await msg.delete()

Each method maps to the Telegram API call you'd otherwise write by hand with ids and chat references.

docs.title: What supports chaining
docs.text:
Chaining comes from message-sending Api methods — sendMessage, sendPhoto, and similar. Not every Api call returns a chainable object. getMe gives you data; sendMessage gives you something you can keep working with.

If you're unsure, await the send and try — if chaining methods exist on the result, you're good.

docs.title: Editing and updating
docs.text:
• editText(text, {...options})
  • editCaption(caption, {...options})
  • editMedia(media, {...options})
  • editReplyMarkup(rm, {...options})

docs.title: Message control
docs.text:
• delete()
  • pin(dn = false) — pass dn: true to pin silently
  • unpin()

docs.title: Reactions
docs.text: • react(emoji, big = false)

docs.title: Forwarding and copying
docs.text:
• forward(to, {...options})
  • copy(to, {...options})

docs.title: Reply methods
docs.text:
• reply(text, {...options})
  • replyPhoto(photo, {...options})
  • replyVideo(video, {...options})
  • replyAudio(audio, {...options})
  • replyVoice(voice, {...options})
  • replyDocument(doc, {...options})
  • replySticker(sticker, {...options})
  • replyAnimation(anim, {...options})
  • replyLocation(lat, lon, {...options})
  • replyContact(phone, fn, {...options})
  • replyPoll(q, options, {...options})
  • replyDice(emoji = "", {...options})

docs.title: Info and utilities
docs.text:
• get() — message id and metadata
  • downloadFile() — download URL for attached media, if any

docs.title: Live location and polls
docs.text:
• editLiveLocation(lat, lon, {...options})
  • stopLiveLocation({...options})
  • stopPoll({...options})

docs.title: Tiny example
docs.text:
let msg = await Api.sendMessage({ text: "Temporary." })
await msg.editText("This will disappear.")
await msg.delete()

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Editing Messages — same edits via standalone Api calls
  • Async Requests — why await matters here

Note

Chaining only applies to message-sending Api responses. Other methods return plain response objects.

docs.title: Sending Messages
docs.text:
The most common thing a bot does is send text. In TBL that's one call:

Api.sendMessage({ text: "Hello." })

No chat_id unless you're deliberately sending somewhere else. TBL uses the chat where the command was triggered.

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
Telegram supports Markdown and HTML in messages. Pick one with parse_mode:

Api.sendMessage({
  text: "*Order confirmed.*\nTracking: `ABC-123`",
  parse_mode: "Markdown"
})

Keep formatting simple. Unclosed bold markers or nested styles are the usual reason a message fails to send. If a formatted message keeps erroring, strip the markup and add it back piece by piece.

docs.title: Sending to a different chat
docs.text:
Sometimes you need to notify an admin channel or message a user from a background command:

Api.sendMessage({
  chat_id: 123456789,
  text: "New signup from the website."
})

Only do this when you're sure the bot can post in that chat — it's a member of the group, hasn't been blocked by the user, etc. Telegram will reject the call otherwise, and by default that rejection lands in your error logs rather than crashing the command.

docs.title: Silent sends
docs.text:
Pass disable_notification: true if the message shouldn't buzz the user's phone:

Api.sendMessage({
  text: "Background sync finished.",
  disable_notification: true
})

Useful for admin alerts in busy groups.

docs.title: Getting a handle on the message
docs.text:
If your next line needs to edit or delete what you just sent, await the call:

let msg = await Api.sendMessage({ text: "Working..." })
// later
await msg.editText("Finished.")

See Method Chaining for everything you can do with that returned object.

docs.title: Handing off to another command
docs.text:
When the response matters but you don't want the rest of the logic in this command:

Api.getChat({ chat_id: chat.id, on_run: "afterGetChat" })

The afterGetChat command receives Telegram's response in options. Callbacks covers that pattern properly.

docs.title: Everything else Telegram supports
docs.text:
Api.sendMessage accepts any parameter the Telegram Bot API documents — reply markup, link previews, protected content, message threading in groups, the lot.

If you need buttons under the message, read Inline Keyboards. For files and media, Media and Files.

docs.title: Tips and Limitations
docs.text: A few things about Api that aren't obvious until they bite you.

docs.title: Two different kinds of errors
docs.text:
You typo'd the method name.

Api.hitMe()

TBL doesn't recognize hitMe. That's a runtime error in your command — execution stops, and your ! handler can catch it if you've defined one.

Telegram rejected a valid call.

Wrong chat, user blocked the bot, bad parameter — the method existed, the request reached Telegram, Telegram said no. That usually doesn't throw. The command keeps going. The failure is logged in TeleBotHost's error panel.

If the failure matters to your logic, use await and inspect ok:

let res = await Api.sendMessage({ text: "Reminder." })

if (!res.ok) {
  // handle it — maybe the user blocked you
}

docs.title: Prefer built-in methods
docs.text: If Api.sendMessage exists, use it. Reach for Api.call("sendMessage", {...}) only when TBL hasn't added a wrapper yet. Built-in methods are easier to read and less typo-prone.

docs.title: Case sensitivity
docs.text: Api.sendMessage works. Api.sendmessage doesn't. Same for every method name.

docs.title: Chat context
docs.text: Most calls assume the current chat. Explicit chat_id overrides that — and introduces a new way to get it wrong. Double-check the bot is actually allowed to message that chat.

docs.title: Always have a ! command
docs.text: Not Api-specific, but worth repeating: define the ! error handler command. Something goes wrong in production, users see a message instead of silence.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
When in doubt, cross-check parameters against the Telegram Bot API docs. TBL passes them through faithfully.

For methods Telegram has but TBL hasn't wrapped yet, see Dynamic Methods.

docs.title: Bot
docs.text:
Bot is TeleBotHost's shortcut for running your bot — not for wrestling with Telegram's API surface.

Where Api mirrors Telegram method-for-method, Bot wraps the things bot authors do every day: send a quick reply, jump to another command, store a setting, pull a list of users. Less boilerplate, fewer parameters you can get wrong.

It's there in every command, same as Api. Just call it.

docs.title: What people actually use it for
docs.text:
Moving between commands. A survey bot finishes step three and needs step four:

Bot.runCommand("/step4")

Pass data along with the second argument — it shows up as options in the target command.

Simple sends. When you don't need inline keyboards or edit-in-place:

Bot.sendMessage("Your code is 48291. It expires in 10 minutes.")

Bot-wide storage. Settings that apply to the whole bot, not one user — feature flags, API keys you've stored, cached totals. See Storing Data.

User lists. Who's used the bot, filtered by chat type or premium status. Listing Users.

docs.title: Case sensitivity
docs.text: Methods are case-sensitive. Bot.runCommand yes, Bot.runcommand no.

docs.title: Bot and Api together
docs.text:
Common pattern: Api handles the Telegram UI (edit the menu message, answer the callback), Bot handles what happens next (run the command that processes the order).

The Bot vs Api guide has a full walkthrough.

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text:
Page Covers Running Commands runCommand, passing options Reading Commands Inspect another command's code or config Sending Messages Text, keyboards, media via Bot Storing Data Key-value storage at bot level Listing Users Query users who've interacted

If you're sending inline buttons or editing messages after send, you'll still need Api for that part.

docs.title: Getting Bot Users
docs.text:
Bot.getUsers() returns an array of user or chat IDs that have interacted with your bot.

This method returns a Promise, so it must be awaited.

It removes the need to manually store user IDs in bot properties.

Info

This feature is available in TBL but is not 100% stable yet.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Get all users who interacted with the bot:

let data = await Bot.getUsers()
  • Return type: Array
  • Must be awaited
  • By default, channel IDs are excluded

You can use the result directly:

Bot.sendMessage({ text: data })

docs.title: Available Filters
docs.text: Filters are optional. If no filter is provided, all users are returned (excluding channels).

docs.title: chatType
docs.text:
Filter by chat type:

  • private
  • group
  • channel

docs.title: premiumOnly
docs.text: Filter only premium users (only applies to private chats)

docs.title: Get Only Group Chats
docs.text:
let groupUsers = await Bot.getUsers({
  chatType: "group"
})

docs.title: Get Only Private Chats
docs.text:
let privateUsers = await Bot.getUsers({
  chatType: "private"
})

docs.title: Get Only Premium Users
docs.text:
let premiumUsers = await Bot.getUsers({
  premiumOnly: true
})

These results contain private chat IDs only.

docs.title: Sending Results
docs.text:
Bot.sendMessage("Group users: " + groupUsers.length)
Bot.sendMessage("Premium users: " + premiumUsers.length)

docs.title: Channel IDs Note
docs.text:
Note

By default, channel IDs are excluded.

To include channels, you must explicitly use:

chatType: "channel"

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• Bot.getUsers() must be awaited
  • Returns an array of IDs
  • Filters are optional
  • Channel chats are excluded by default
  • Feature is still under development

docs.title: Reading Commands and Their Code
docs.text:
TBL allows you to read existing commands programmatically using the Bot instance.

This is useful for:

  • Debugging command logic
  • Building admin or moderation tools
  • Showing command previews
  • Creating documentation bots
  • Auditing or inspecting commands safely

docs.title: Reading Command Code Only
docs.text:
The Bot.read() method returns only the raw source code of a command.

It does not include command settings like answer, keyboard, aliases, or reply behavior.

The returned value is a plain string.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
// Read the raw code of a command
let code = Bot.read("/start")

// it returns a String

Use this when you only care about how the command works internally.

Tip

Bot.read() is ideal for code previews, AI analysis, or debugging logic issues.

docs.title: Reading Full Command Object
docs.text:
The Bot.readCommand() method returns the entire command definition.

This includes:

  • The command code
  • Answer text
  • Keyboard configuration
  • Aliases
  • need_reply flag
  • Other command settings

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
// Read full command structure
let cmd = Bot.readCommand("/start")

docs.title: Example Response
docs.text:
{
  "code": "const {random} = require(\"/send\");\n\nconst x = random(1, 100);\nBot.sendMessage(\"Random: \" + x);",
  "answer": null,
  "keyboard": null,
  "aliases": [],
  "allow_only_group": false,
  "need_reply": false
}

Use this when you need both the logic and the configuration of a command.

Info

Bot.readCommand() is commonly used in admin panels, editors, and bot management systems.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• Both methods are read-only
  • The target command must exist
  • Missing commands will throw an error
  • Errors can be handled using the ! command
  • Returned data never executes automatically

docs.title: Command Execution
docs.text:
The Bot instance allows you to execute another command programmatically.

This is useful when you want to:

  • Move a user to a new flow
  • Reuse existing commands
  • Control navigation inside your bot

These methods do not return any value — they only execute the target command.

docs.title: Running Another Command
docs.text: You can run another command directly using Bot.runCommand.

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
// Run another command
Bot.runCommand("/start")

This immediately executes the /start command.

docs.title: Running a Command with Options
docs.text:
You can pass custom data to the target command.

// Run with options

/*
Bot.runCommand("command", options)
*/

Bot.runCommand("/ok", { key: 111 })

Inside the /ok command, this data is available as options

docs.title: Options Availability
docs.text:
• The passed object is available as options in the target command
  • You can pass any JSON-serializable data
  • Useful for sharing state between commands

docs.title: Invalid Command Handling
docs.text:
If the target command does not exist:

  • A runtime error is thrown
  • The error can be caught using the ! command
  • Execution stops unless handled

Warning

Running a non-existent command will throw an error unless explicitly told not to.

docs.title: Advanced Command Execution
docs.text:
For more control, you can use Bot.run().

This allows you to define execution behavior using an options object.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Bot.run({
  command: "/contact"
})

docs.title: command (required)
docs.text:
• The command to execute
  • Example: /start
  • You can include parameters in the command string

docs.title: options
docs.text:
• A JSON object passed to the target command
  • Available as options inside that command

docs.title: user_id
docs.text:
• User ID to execute the command for
  • Default: current user.id

docs.title: chat_id
docs.text:
• Chat ID to execute the command in
  • Default: current chat.id

docs.title: ignoreMissingCommand
docs.text:
• If true, no error is thrown when the command is not found
  • Default: false

docs.title: Example with Full Options
docs.text:
Bot.run({
  command: "/next",
  options: { step: 2 },
  user_id: 123456789,
  chat_id: 987654321,
  ignoreMissingCommand: true
})

docs.title: When to Use ignoreMissingCommand
docs.text:
This option is useful when:

  • Running optional commands
  • Building fallback logic
  • Working with system commands like @ or *

Tip

Use ignoreMissingCommand carefully. Silently skipping commands can make debugging harder.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Bot.runCommand() runs a command directly
  • Bot.run() provides advanced control
  • Options are passed through options
  • Missing commands throw errors by default
  • Errors can be handled using the ! command

docs.title: Sending Messages and Media with Bot
docs.text:
These Bot methods send messages or media to the current chat.

  • All messages go to the current chat by default
  • Using await is optional
  • If awaited, the Telegram API response is returned
  • Only some methods support chained actions

docs.title: Simple Text
docs.text: Bot.sendMessage("Hello user!")

docs.title: Object Format
docs.text: Bot.sendMessage({ text: "Hello user!" })

docs.title: With Formatting
docs.text:
let res = await Bot.sendMessage(
  "Hello friend",
  { parse_mode: "HTML" }
)

docs.title: String Format
docs.text: Bot.sendKeyboard("Choose an option:", "Yes,No")

docs.title: Object Format
docs.text:
Bot.sendKeyboard({
  text: "Choose an option:",
  keyboard: "Yes,No"
})

docs.title: Sending Media
docs.text: All media methods support string and object formats.

docs.title: Photo
docs.text:
Bot.sendPhoto("photo.jpg")

Bot.sendPhoto({
  photo: "photo.jpg",
  caption: "Nice view!"
})

docs.title: Document
docs.text:
Bot.sendDocument("file.pdf", "Here is your pdf")

Bot.sendDocument({
  document: "file.pdf",
  caption: "Here is your file"
})

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
Bot.sendAudio("music.mp3")

Bot.sendAudio({
  audio: "music.mp3",
  caption: "Here is your music"
})

docs.title: Video
docs.text:
Bot.sendVideo("video.mp4")

Bot.sendVideo({
  video: "video.mp4",
  caption: "Watch this"
})

docs.title: Voice
docs.text:
Bot.sendVoice("voice.ogg")

Bot.sendVoice({
  voice: "voice.ogg",
  caption: "Voice note"
})

docs.title: Using Chained Methods (Limited Support)
docs.text:
Only specific Bot methods return a response that supports chained methods (when used with await).

Example:

let data = await Bot.sendMessage("Pinned message")

data.pin()

Note

Not all Bot methods support chaining. Chaining works only when the method returns a Telegram message object.

docs.title: Debugging with Bot.inspect()
docs.text:
Bot.inspect() sends inspect data to the current chat.

It is mainly used for debugging and checking values quickly.

docs.title: Inspect Any Data
docs.text: Bot.inspect({ user: "Alice", id: 123 })

docs.title: Inspect Multiple Values
docs.text:
Bot.inspect(
  "User data:",
  user,
  { id: 123 },
  someArray
)

The inspected data is formatted and sent as a message in the chat.

Tip

Use Bot.inspect() only during development. Avoid using it in production bots for users.

docs.title: Available Bot Methods
docs.text:
Only the following Bot methods are available for sending output:

  • Bot.sendMessage
  • Bot.sendKeyboard
  • Bot.sendDocument
  • Bot.sendPhoto
  • Bot.sendAudio
  • Bot.sendVideo
  • Bot.sendVoice
  • Bot.inspect

These methods are intentionally limited and focused on output and flow control.

docs.title: Not Available in Bot
docs.text:
Methods that read or query Telegram data, such as:

  • getChat
  • getMe
  • getUserProfilePhotos
  • or similar Telegram API read methods

are not available in the Bot instance.

Info

The Bot instance is designed for sending responses and controlling bot behavior, not for querying Telegram data.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• All Bot send methods use the current chat
  • await is optional
  • Only limited methods support chained actions
  • Bot.inspect() sends output to chat
  • Method names are case-sensitive
  • Errors can be handled using the ! command

docs.title: Bot Data Store
docs.text:
The Bot Data Store is a simple key–value storage that belongs to the bot itself.

It is not user-specific and not chat-specific. Anything stored here is shared across the entire bot.

All data store methods are synchronous, so you do not need await.

docs.title: Setting Data
docs.text:
You can store values using Bot.set().

// Set values
Bot.set("version", "1.2.3", "String")
Bot.set("config", { apiKey: "xyz" }, "Json")
  • The first argument is the key
  • The second argument is the value
  • The third argument is the data type (optional)

Info

If the type is not provided, TBL automatically detects it.

docs.title: Reading Data
docs.text:
You can read stored values using Bot.get().

let v = Bot.get("version")   // "1.2.3"
let c = Bot.get("config")    // { apiKey: "xyz" }

If the key does not exist, the result will be null.

docs.title: Deleting Data
docs.text:
Delete a single key:

Bot.del("version")

Delete all stored data:

Bot.delAll()

Warning

Bot.delAll() permanently removes all bot-level data. Use it carefully.

docs.title: Checking Existence
docs.text:
Check if a key exists:

let has = Bot.has("config")  // true

This is useful before reading or overwriting values.

docs.title: Listing Stored Data
docs.text:
Get all stored key–value pairs:

let all = Bot.getAll()

Get the total number of stored keys:

let count = Bot.count()

Get all stored key names:

let names = Bot.getNames()   // ["config"]

docs.title: Supported Data Types
docs.text:
The following data types are supported:

  • String – Plain text or auto-converted values
  • Number – Integers or floats
  • Boolean – true or false
  • List – Arrays (ordered lists)
  • Date – Date objects
  • json – Objects or arrays stored as json

Note

When storing complex data, json is recommended for consistency.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• Data is stored at the bot level
  • Values persist across command executions
  • Data is shared between all users
  • Methods are synchronous
  • Keys are case-sensitive

Tip

Use the Bot Data Store for configuration, feature flags, counters, or bot state — not for user-specific data.

docs.title: Using Aliases in Your Bot
docs.text: Aliases allow a single command to be triggered using multiple names. They make bots more flexible and easier to use.

docs.title: What is an Alias?
docs.text:
An alias is an alternative trigger for a command.

This means:

  • One command
  • Multiple triggers
  • Same behavior every time

docs.title: Why Aliases Are Useful
docs.text:
Aliases help you:

  • Support different typing styles
  • Match keyboard button text
  • Provide short and long command names
  • Reduce user mistakes

They improve usability without adding logic.

docs.title: Where Aliases Are Used
docs.text:
Aliases are defined inside a command’s configuration.

When a message arrives, TBL checks:

  • The command name
  • Then its aliases
  • Then other matching rules

Aliases behave exactly like the main command.

docs.title: Adding Aliases to a Command
docs.text:
Open an existing command and add values in the Aliases field.

Each alias is treated as a separate trigger for the same command.

Note

Aliases are case-sensitive. Help, help, and HELP are treated as different triggers.

If you want to support multiple cases, you must add each variation as a separate alias.

docs.title: Aliases and Keyboards
docs.text:
Aliases work perfectly with keyboards.

For example:

  • A keyboard button labeled Help
  • An alias named Help

Both trigger the same command.

Tip

Always add an alias that exactly matches your keyboard button text.

docs.title: Best Practices for Aliases
docs.text:
Follow these guidelines:

  • Keep aliases short and clear
  • Match keyboard labels exactly
  • Avoid overlapping aliases across commands
  • Add only meaningful alternatives

Tip

Fewer, well-chosen aliases are better than many confusing ones.

docs.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
docs.text:
Avoid:

  • Using the same alias in multiple commands
  • Adding unrelated words as aliases
  • Forgetting case variations when needed

Aliases should always point clearly to one command.

docs.title: Test Your Aliases
docs.text:
After adding aliases:

  • Open your bot in Telegram
  • Try typing different alias forms
  • Tap keyboard buttons
  • Confirm they all trigger the same response

If everything works, your aliases are set up correctly.

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
With aliases, you now know how to:

  • Trigger one command in multiple ways
  • Connect keyboards and text input
  • Improve usability without logic

docs.title: Adding a Keyboard to Your Bot
docs.text:
Now let’s improve our first bot by adding a keyboard.

Keyboards allow users to tap buttons instead of typing commands. This makes bots easier to use and more user-friendly.

docs.title: What We Are Building
docs.text:
We will update the /start command to:

  • Send a welcome message
  • Show buttons on the screen
  • Let users choose what to do next

docs.title: What is a Keyboard?
docs.text:
A keyboard is a set of buttons shown below the message input field.

When a user taps a button, the button text is sent back to the bot as a normal message.

This means:

  • No typing required
  • Fewer mistakes
  • Better user experience

docs.title: Step 1 — Open the Command
docs.text:
• Go to your bot panel on TeleBotHost
  • Open the Commands section
  • Find the existing /start command
  • Click the pencil (edit) icon to update it

docs.title: Step 2 — Add the Keyboard
docs.text:
Update the command fields like this:

Command: /start

Answer: Hello 👋 Choose one of the options below to continue.

Keyboard : Help, About

This creates two buttons in a single row.

docs.title: Keyboard Layout Basics
docs.text:
Keyboards are simple to define using text.

  • Buttons in the same row are separated by commas
  • New rows are created using a new line

Warning

A keyboard always requires an Answer. Buttons cannot be sent without a message, so make sure the Answer field is filled whenever you use a keyboard.

Examples:

  • Yes,No → one row with two buttons
  • Yes\nNo → two rows with one button each
  • Yes,No\nBoth → two rows: first row Yes, No, second row Both

Tip

You can mix rows and button counts freely to design your menu.

docs.title: How Keyboard Buttons Work
docs.text:
When a user taps a keyboard button:

  • Telegram sends the button text as a message
  • TBL treats it like normal text input
  • A matching command can respond to it

For example, tapping Help sends the message Help.

docs.title: Creating the Help Command
docs.text:
Now let’s make the Help button actually do something.

Add a new command with these details:

Command : Help

Answer : Here’s what I can help you with: - Use the buttons to navigate - Tap About to learn more about me - Send /start anytime to restart

No logic is needed yet.

docs.title: Creating the About Command
docs.text:
Next, create the About command.

Add another command with:

Command : About

Answer : I’m a simple Telegram bot built using TBL on TeleBotHost. I use commands and keyboards to guide users easily.

This gives users basic information about your bot.

docs.title: Why Keyboards Are Useful
docs.text:
Keyboards are great for:

  • Menus
  • Navigation
  • Guided user flows
  • Reducing confusion for new users

Tip

Use keyboards for common actions instead of forcing users to remember commands.

docs.title: Test the Keyboard and Commands
docs.text:
• Open your bot in Telegram
  • Send /start
  • You should see the buttons
  • Tap Help and About
  • Each button should show its response

If everything works, your bot menu is complete 🎉

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
With this update, you learned:

  • How to add a keyboard to a command
  • How keyboard buttons send text messages
  • How to handle buttons using normal commands
  • How to build a simple menu-based bot

docs.title: What’s Next
docs.text:
Next, you can:

  • Add a Back button
  • Create multi-level menus
  • Combine keyboards with reply-based input
  • Add logic to commands

Your bot is now interactive and user-friendly.

docs.title: Commands in TBL
docs.text:
Commands are the foundation of how bots work in TBL (Tele Bot Lang). Every action, response, or behavior in a TeleBotHost bot is driven by a command.

TBL does not rely on event listeners or long-running background processes. Instead, it follows a command-driven execution model, where each incoming update triggers exactly one command.

docs.title: What is a Command?
docs.text:
A command is a rule that defines what the bot should do when a specific trigger is matched.

For every incoming update:

  • Telegram sends an update to the bot
  • TBL inspects the update
  • A matching command is selected
  • That command is executed
  • Execution ends cleanly

Only one command runs per update.

Info

TBL never executes multiple commands automatically for a single update.

docs.title: Slash Commands
docs.text:
Slash commands start with /, such as /start.

They are commonly used for:

  • Entry points
  • User onboarding
  • Explicit user actions

docs.title: Text-Based Commands
docs.text:
Commands can also be triggered by plain text messages.

They are useful for:

  • Menu-driven bots
  • Keyword-based replies
  • Conversational flows

Text-based commands behave exactly the same as slash commands.

docs.title: Button and Interaction Triggers
docs.text:
Commands may also be triggered by user interactions, such as:

  • Reply keyboards
  • Inline buttons
  • Menu selections

These triggers help guide users and reduce manual typing.

docs.title: Inline Query Commands
docs.text:
Inline query commands handle Telegram inline mode, when users type @yourbot query inside any chat.

These commands are useful for:

  • Search-style bots
  • Inline tools
  • Quick content insertion

Inline queries are handled by a dedicated command.

docs.title: Command Matching Order
docs.text:
TBL uses a strict and predictable matching order.

When an update arrives, commands are checked in this order:

  • Exact command name
  • Aliases
  • Dynamic update handlers
  • Fallback command

This ensures that specific logic always runs before generic logic.

Tip

A strict matching order makes command behavior predictable and easier to debug.

docs.title: Command Parts
docs.text: Each command can include multiple optional parts. These parts define how the command behaves.

docs.title: Command Name
docs.text:
The command name defines the trigger.

It can be:

  • A slash command
  • A keyword
  • A system identifier

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
An answer is a static message sent immediately when the command is triggered.

It is useful for:

  • Quick responses
  • Simple instructions
  • Instant feedback

The answer is always sent before any command logic runs.

docs.title: Logic (Bot Main Codes)
docs.text:
The logic defines what the bot actually does after the command is triggered.

Typical responsibilities include:

  • Sending messages
  • Processing user input
  • Calling external APIs
  • Saving or reading data
  • Triggering other commands

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
Aliases allow a command to be triggered using multiple names.

They are useful for:

  • Handling typos
  • Supporting multiple languages
  • Creating shortcuts

All aliases behave exactly the same as the main command.

docs.title: Keyboard
docs.text:
Commands can optionally display keyboards.

Keyboards help:

  • Reduce typing
  • Guide user actions
  • Improve user experience

They are shown only when explicitly defined.

docs.title: Need Reply
docs.text:
Some commands expect a follow-up message from the user.

When enabled:

  • The bot waits for the next user message
  • That message becomes the input
  • The command flow continues

Warning

Overusing reply-based commands can confuse users and make flows harder to manage.

docs.title: /start — Entry Command
docs.text:
The /start command is the primary entry point for users.

It is typically used for:

  • Welcoming users
  • Explaining bot features
  • Resetting user flow

While not mandatory, it is strongly recommended.

docs.title: @ — Initialization Command
docs.text:
The @ command runs before any other command.

It is used for:

  • Preparing global data
  • Defining helper logic
  • Setting shared configuration

Info

The @ command runs on every update and executes before command matching.

Tip

This command has advanced use cases that will be covered later.

docs.title: ! — Error Handler Command
docs.text:
The ! command runs when a runtime error occurs during command execution.

It is used for:

  • Handling failures gracefully
  • Sending error messages
  • Preventing silent crashes

Warning

Always define a ! command to handle unexpected errors safely.

docs.title: @@ — Post-Processing Command
docs.text:
The @@ command runs after every command execution, whether it succeeds or fails.

It is commonly used for:

  • Cleanup tasks
  • Logging
  • Analytics
  • Post-execution actions

docs.title: * — Fallback (Wildcard) Command
docs.text:
The * command runs when no other command matches.

It acts as:

  • A default handler
  • A safety net
  • A universal fallback

Warning

Not defining a fallback command may cause some updates to be ignored.

docs.title: /inline_query — Inline Mode Handler
docs.text:
The /inline_query command handles inline queries triggered by users typing @yourbot query inside chats.

It is responsible for:

  • Reading inline query input
  • Returning inline results
  • Powering search-style interactions

If /inline_query is not defined, inline updates fall back to the * command.

docs.title: /channel_update — Channel Post Handler
docs.text:
The /channel_update command handles channel-related updates automatically.

It is used for:

  • Channel posts
  • Channel edits
  • Channel-related events

If this command is not defined, channel updates fall back to the * command.

docs.title: Dynamic Commands
docs.text:
TBL supports dynamic commands that handle specific Telegram update types automatically.

Dynamic commands follow a fixed naming pattern:

  • /handle_{update_type}

Examples include:

  • /handle_channel_post
  • /handle_chat_member
  • /handle_poll_answer
  • /handle_message_reaction

These commands are triggered automatically when the corresponding Telegram update is received.

If a dynamic command is not defined:

  • Channel-related updates fall back to /channel_update
  • All other updates fall back to *

Info

Dynamic commands remove the need for manual update parsing or event listeners.

docs.title: Final Command Execution Flow
docs.text:
Every update in TBL follows the same execution order:

  • The update is received
  • The @ initialization command runs
  • A matching command runs
  • The ! command runs only if an error occurs
  • The @@ command runs after execution
  • Execution ends

Flow summary:

Update → @ → matched command → ! (on error) → @@ → end

docs.title: Good Practices
docs.text:
• Use clear and meaningful command names
  • Keep one responsibility per command
  • Always define ! and *
  • Use aliases thoughtfully
  • Prefer dynamic commands for system updates
  • Keep reply-based flows short and clear

docs.title: What to Avoid
docs.text:
Avoid:

  • Overloading a single command with too much logic
  • Creating deep or confusing reply chains
  • Relying on fallback commands for core features
  • Ignoring error handling
  • Creating ambiguous or overlapping triggers

docs.title: Why This Model Works
docs.text:
TBL’s command system is intentionally focused and restricted.

This design:

  • Improves security
  • Prevents unexpected behavior
  • Makes bots easier to understand
  • Scales reliably under high traffic

Instead of managing events and listeners, developers define clear reactions to specific triggers, resulting in predictable and maintainable bots.

docs.title: Your First Bot
docs.text:
Let's get something working on Telegram in the next few minutes.

The bot will respond to /start with a hello message. No logic field required — just a command name and an answer.

docs.title: Open the command editor
docs.text:
Dashboard → your bot → Commands → Add Command.

Everything your bot does lives here.

docs.title: Fill in two fields
docs.text:
Command: /start

Answer:

Hello 👋
Welcome to my first TBL bot!

Save it. That's the whole bot for now.

docs.title: What happens when someone types /start
docs.text: Telegram delivers the update. TBL matches /start, sends the answer, done. The answer goes out before any logic runs — so for simple replies you often don't need a logic field at all.

docs.title: Formatting the answer
docs.text:
The answer field accepts Telegram Markdown. Bold, italic, line breaks — useful for welcome text.

*Welcome!*
Choose an option below.

Start plain. Add formatting once the message sends reliably.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
Open your bot in Telegram, send /start. You should see the hello message right away.

If nothing comes back, check the bot is launched in the dashboard and you're messaging the correct bot username.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
Adding a Keyboard — give users buttons so they don't have to type commands.

Or read Command Structure if you want the full picture of how triggers and special commands work.

docs.title: Handling User Input with Need Reply
docs.text:
Now that your bot can respond to commands and keyboards, the next step is handling user input.

This is done using Need Reply, which allows a command to wait for the user’s next message before continuing.

docs.title: What is Need Reply?
docs.text:
Need Reply tells the bot to pause and wait for the user’s next message.

Instead of finishing immediately, the command stays active until the user replies.

This is useful when you need input like:

  • A name
  • A value
  • A choice
  • Any simple user response

docs.title: Simple Input Example
docs.text:
We will create a command that asks for the user’s name and replies using that input.

Command : /input

Answer : Tell me your name 🙂

Need Reply : true

Logic (TBL Code) 

Bot.sendMessage("Your name is " + message)

docs.title: How This Works
docs.text:
Step by step:

  • User sends /input
  • The bot replies: “Tell me your name”
  • Because Need Reply is enabled, the bot waits
  • User sends their next message
  • That message is captured
  • The logic runs and replies using the input

The important rule is this:

The next message is treated as input, not as a new command.

docs.title: What message Means Here
docs.text:
For this beginner example:

  • message refers only to the text sent by the user
  • It does not handle media or other message types
  • This keeps the bot simple and easy to understand

Note

Advanced bots can handle all update types, but for learning purposes, message is treated as plain text here.

docs.title: How to Cancel Need Reply
docs.text:
Sometimes a user may change their mind or want to stop the input process.

To cancel Need Reply, the user can simply send any valid existing command.

For example:

  • /start
  • Help
  • About

When a valid command is received:

  • The waiting state is cleared
  • Need Reply is cancelled
  • Normal command matching resumes

Info

Sending a valid command automatically cancels the active Need Reply state.

This makes it easy for users to escape input mode without getting stuck.

docs.title: Why This Is Important
docs.text:
Without a cancel option:

  • Users can feel trapped
  • Other commands stop working temporarily
  • The bot feels broken

Allowing users to send a valid command keeps the bot safe and user-friendly.

docs.title: Good Practices for Need Reply
docs.text:
Follow these rules:

  • Always explain what input you expect
  • Keep reply flows short
  • Allow users to cancel using /start or menu buttons
  • Respond immediately after receiving input
  • Avoid chaining many reply-based steps

Warning

Leaving users in a reply-waiting state without clear instructions can block normal bot usage.

docs.title: Test the Cancel Behavior
docs.text:
To test cancellation:

  • Send /input
  • Instead of replying with text, send /start
  • The bot should cancel the input flow and restart normally

If this works, your Need Reply handling is correct.

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
With Need Reply, you now understand how to:

  • Pause a command and wait for input
  • Read simple text input using message
  • Cancel input mode safely
  • Build basic interactive flows

This is the foundation for setup wizards, forms, and guided user interactions.

docs.title: Using the Wildcard (*) Command
docs.text:
Now let’s build a bot that always replies, no matter what the user sends.

This is done using the wildcard command (*).

docs.title: What is the * Command?
docs.text:
The * command is a catch-all command.

It runs when:

  • No other command matches
  • The input is unknown
  • The user sends random text or commands

In simple words:

If nothing else matches, * runs.

docs.title: What We Are Building
docs.text:
We will create a bot that:

  • Replies to any message
  • Does not require specific commands
  • Always sends the same answer

This is useful for simple auto-reply bots or fallback responses.

docs.title: Step 1 — Create the Command
docs.text:
Open your bot’s Commands section and add a new command.

Command : * Answer : Hello 👋 I reply to everything you send!

That’s it. No logic is required.

docs.title: How the * Command Works
docs.text:
When a user sends any message:

  • TBL checks all defined commands
  • If no command matches
  • The * command is selected
  • The answer is sent

This happens for:

  • Normal text
  • Unknown commands
  • Random input
  • All Telegram update types

Tip

The * command can capture all Telegram update types when no other command matches.

docs.title: Example Behavior
docs.text:
With only the * command defined:

  • User sends Hi → bot replies
  • User sends /test → bot replies
  • User sends anything → bot replies

The same answer is sent every time.

Info

The * command only runs when no other command matches.

docs.title: * With Other Commands
docs.text:
If your bot also has a /start command:

  • /start → /start command runs
  • Anything else → * command runs

This makes * perfect as a fallback.

docs.title: Good Use Cases
docs.text:
Use the * command for:

  • Default replies
  • Unknown input handling
  • Help prompts
  • Maintenance messages

Warning

Do not place important bot logic inside *. Use it as a fallback, not a primary command.

docs.title: Test the Bot
docs.text:
• Open your bot in Telegram
  • Send any message
  • The bot should always reply

If it does, your wildcard command is working 🎉

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
You now understand how:

  • The * command works
  • To build an always-replying bot
  • To handle unknown input safely
  • To use * as a fallback command

docs.title: Global Instance
docs.text:
The Global instance is used to store and manage data at the account level.

All data stored using the Global instance is shared across all bots under the same owner account.

Any bot belonging to the account can read or modify this data.

This is useful for:

  • Shared configuration across bots
  • Account-wide settings
  • Common flags or counters
  • Data that should not belong to a single bot or user

Global data is scoped to the owner account, not to an individual bot or user.

docs.title: Basic Global Operations
docs.text:
Use the Global instance to store and read data at the account level.

All operations here use the string-based method format and apply to the entire owner account.

Data stored here is shared across all bots under the same account.

docs.title: Saving Global Data
docs.text:
Use Global.set() to store values.

Global.set("version", "1.0.0")
Global.set("max_limit", 100, "number")
  • First argument: key
  • Second argument: value
  • Third argument (optional): data type

If the type is not provided, it is auto-detected.

docs.title: Reading Global Data
docs.text:
Use Global.get() to read stored values.

let version = Global.get("version")
let limit = Global.get("max_limit")

Bot.sendMessage("Version: " + version + ", Limit: " + limit)

Reading data is synchronous and returns the value directly.

If a key does not exist, it returns null.

docs.title: Deleting a Single Value
docs.text:
Remove a specific global value.

Global.del("max_limit")

let limit = Global.get("max_limit")   // null
Bot.sendMessage("After delete, limit = " + limit)

Deleting a non-existing key does nothing and does not throw an error.

docs.title: Bulk Operations
docs.text:
Bulk operations let you work with all global data at once.

These are useful for inspecting or resetting account-level data.

docs.title: Get All Global Data
docs.text:
let all = Global.getAll()
Bot.inspect(all)

Example output:

{
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "maintenance": false
}

This returns an object containing all stored global keys and values.

docs.title: Delete All Global Data
docs.text:
Global.delAll()

let all2 = Global.getAll()
Bot.inspect(all2)

This clears all global data for the account.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Data is stored at the account level
  • Shared across all bots under the same owner
  • Only string-based methods are used here
  • Reading (get, getAll) is synchronous
  • Saving and deleting do not require await
  • Missing keys always return null

docs.title: Storage Monitoring
docs.text:
The Global instance can be used to monitor storage usage at the account level.

It gives visibility into total storage consumed across:

  • Bot data
  • User data
  • Global data

This helps you track usage, prevent limits from being reached, and plan cleanups.

docs.title: Get Detailed Storage Information
docs.text:
Retrieve detailed storage stats for your account.

let storageInfo = Global.getStorageInfo()
Bot.inspect(storageInfo)

Example output:

{
  "size": 1572864,
  "prop_count": 42,
  "last_calc": "2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z"
}
  • size → total storage used (bytes)
  • prop_count → total stored entries
  • last_calc → last calculation timestamp

docs.title: Get Storage Usage Percentage
docs.text:
Check how much storage is used as a percentage (0–100).

let usagePercent = Global.getStorageUsage()
Bot.sendMessage("Storage usage: " + usagePercent + "%")

This is useful for dashboards or alerts.

docs.title: Check If Storage Is Near Limit
docs.text:
You can quickly detect when storage is close to full.

if (Global.isStorageNearLimit()) {
  Bot.sendMessage("⚠️ Storage almost full! Please clean up some data.")
}

By default, this checks against a 90% threshold.

docs.title: Get Available Storage
docs.text:
Find out how much storage is still available.

let availableMB = Global.getAvailableStorage()
Bot.sendMessage("Available storage: " + availableMB + " MB")

This value is returned in megabytes (MB).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• All storage metrics are account-wide
  • Includes Bot, User, and Global data
  • Useful for monitoring, alerts, and maintenance
  • Helps avoid unexpected storage limits

The Global instance provides a simple way to observe and manage your account’s storage usage.

docs.title: Global Variables
docs.text: TBL provides built-in global variables in every command. They give you access to the current update, user, chat, and runtime context without any setup or imports.

docs.title: How to Use This Section
docs.text: Each variable below is documented on its own page with examples and field descriptions. Variables are read-only during command execution unless noted otherwise.

docs.title: Available Variables
docs.text: Variable Description update Full Telegram update object that triggered the command update_type String name of the update type (e.g. message, callback_query) request Incoming HTTP request data in webhook mode message The message object when the update includes one user The user who triggered the update chat The chat where the update occurred bot Metadata about the current bot owner The bot owner's account information plan The bot owner's subscription plan details params URL query parameters in webhook and Webapp commands options Custom data passed when running a command programmatically tbl_options Internal options set by TBL for HTTP callbacks and flows content Parsed content from the current update msg (global) Shortcut to the current message context (distinct from the msg instance) error Error details inside the ! error handler command http_response Response data from HTTP callback commands process Environment and runtime process information

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• Global variables exist only while a command is running
  • Not every variable is available in every command type (e.g. request is webhook-only)
  • The global msg variable is different from the msg instance — see both pages before using message methods

docs.title: The bot Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, bot contains information about the current bot running the command.

It provides details about the bot’s identity, owner, and platform status.

docs.title: What bot Contains
docs.text:
The bot variable is a JSON object with platform-level information about the bot.

It may include:

  • Internal bot ID on TeleBotHost
  • Telegram bot ID
  • Bot name
  • Owner information
  • Bot status
  • Creation and update timestamps

docs.title: Demo Bot Object
docs.text:
Example structure of the bot object:

{
  "id": 42,
  "token": "123456:ABC...",
  "name": "DemoBot",
  "bot_id": 987654321,
  "owner": "somemail@telebothost.com",
  "status": "working",
  "created_at": "2025-01-01",
  "updated_at": "2025-01-10"
}

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• bot is read-only
  • It exists only during command execution
  • It represents platform-level information, not Telegram updates

The bot variable is useful for admin tools, logging, and bot management logic.

docs.title: The chat Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, chat contains details about the current chat where the interaction happened.

This can be a private chat, group, or channel.

docs.title: What chat Contains
docs.text:
The chat variable is a JSON object that describes the chat context.

It may include information such as:

  • Chat ID
  • Chat type (private, group, channel)
  • Chat username or title
  • Block status
  • Whether the chat was just created

docs.title: Demo Chat Object
docs.text:
Example structure of the chat object:

{
  "id": 5723455420,
  "first_name": "Soumyadeep ∞",
  "username": "soumyadeepdas765",
  "type": "private",
  "chatid": 5723455420,
  "chatId": 5723455420,
  "blocked": false,
  "block_reason": null,
  "blocked_at": null,
  "just_created": true
}

docs.title: When chat Is Available
docs.text:
• For most message-based updates, chat is available
  • For some system or webhook updates, it may be null

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• chat is either an object or null
  • It is read-only
  • It exists only during the current command execution

The chat variable helps your bot understand where the interaction is happening.

docs.title: The content Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, content contains the response body returned from an HTTP request.

It represents the main data received from the server.

docs.title: How content Works
docs.text:
When you make an HTTP request:

  • The response body is converted to text
  • That text is stored in content
  • The value is usually stringified data

For example, if an API returns JSON, content will contain it as a string.

docs.title: Demo Example
docs.text:
Example value of content:

"{\"status\":true,\"message\":\"Hello from API\"}"

You can then parse or process this value in your logic if needed.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• content contains text data
  • It exists only during command execution
  • Its value depends on the HTTP response

The content variable is mainly used when working with external APIs.

docs.title: The error Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, error contains information about an error that was caught by the ! command.

It is only available when an error occurs during command execution.

docs.title: How error Works
docs.text:
• When a runtime error happens, the ! command is triggered
  • Inside the ! command, error becomes available
  • error describes what went wrong

This allows you to handle failures safely.

docs.title: What error Contains
docs.text:
The error variable is an object that may include:

  • Error message
  • Error type
  • Stack information
  • Execution details

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• error is available only inside the ! command and HTTP call fallback command on error
  • It is read-only
  • It exists only during error handling

The error variable helps you debug issues and show user-friendly error messages.

docs.title: The http_response Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, http_response contains full information about an HTTP request result.

It is only available inside HTTP callback commands (commands triggered after an HTTP request completes).

docs.title: When http_response Is Available
docs.text:
• Only for HTTP callback commands
  • Not available in normal message-based commands
  • Automatically provided after an HTTP request finishes

docs.title: What http_response Contains
docs.text:
The http_response variable is an object that includes:

  • Request options
  • HTTP response data
  • Metadata like timestamps

docs.title: Demo http_response Object
docs.text:
Example structure of http_response:

{
  "options": {
    "url": "https://webapi.telebothost.com/",
    "success": "/link"
  },
  "response": {
    "ok": true,
    "status": 200,
    "statusText": "",
    "content": "{\"status\":\"ok\",\"message\":\"API Service Running\"}",
    "data": {
      "status": "ok",
