      "message": "API Service Running"
    },
    "isJson": true,
    "headers": {
      "server": "nginx/1.24.0 (Ubuntu)",
      "content-type": "application/json; charset=utf-8"
    },
    "cookies": [],
    "url": "https://webapi.telebothost.com/",
    "redirected": false,
    "redirectCount": 0
  },
  "timestamp": 1766335656394
}

docs.title: The response Variable
docs.text:
For convenience, TBL also exposes:

  • response → same as http_response.response

This lets you access response details directly without referencing the full object.

docs.title: Commonly Used Response Fields
docs.text:
Inside response, you will often use:

  • response.ok → request success status
  • response.status → HTTP status code
  • response.content → raw response body (string)
  • response.data → parsed JSON data (if available)
  • response.isJson → whether the response was JSON

docs.title: Headers and Cookies
docs.text:
Headers and cookies are also exposed directly.

  • headers → same as response.headers
  • cookies → same as response.cookies

This makes it easier to work with HTTP metadata.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• http_response is read-only
  • It exists only during the callback command execution
  • Structure depends on the HTTP request and response
  • content is always a string, even for JSON responses

The http_response variable is mainly used for API integrations, external services, and data fetching workflows.

docs.title: The message Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, message contains only the text of a message.

Example value: "Hello bot"

docs.title: How message Works
docs.text:
• If the update type is a text message, message contains that text
  • If the update is not a text message, message is null

This means:

  • Text message → message has value
  • Photo, sticker, button, webhook, etc. → message is null

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• message contains text only
  • It does not include media or metadata
  • It exists only during command execution

For simple bots, message is the easiest way to read user input.

docs.title: The msg Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, msg is a simplified version of update that is available only for message updates.

It is designed to make working with normal messages easier.

Not the same as the msg instance

This page documents the global msg variable (read-only message context). For message-sending methods like msg.replyText(), see the msg instance.

docs.title: How msg Works
docs.text:
• When the update type is a message, msg is available
  • msg contains the same object as update.message
  • If the update is not a message, msg is not available

This means you don’t need to access the full update object for common message-based bots.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• msg is available only for message updates
  • It is read-only
  • It exists only during command execution

For simple bots that mainly handle messages, msg is often more convenient than using update.message directly.

docs.title: The options Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, options contains custom data passed between commands or data returned from API callbacks.

It helps share context without using global state.

docs.title: How options Is Used
docs.text:
The options variable is commonly used in two cases:

  • When chaining or triggering another command
  • When receiving the result of a Telegram API call

docs.title: Custom Data Example
docs.text:
When passing custom data between commands, options may look like this:

{
  "name": "Alice",
  "step": 2
}

This is useful for multi-step flows and internal state tracking.

docs.title: API Callback Example
docs.text:
When options comes from a Telegram API response, it may contain result data:

{
  "ok": true,
  "result": { }
}

The options variable is mainly used for advanced flows and integrations.

docs.title: The owner Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, owner contains information about the bot owner.

It provides details such as the owner’s email, subscription plan, and API keys used for platform-level integrations.

docs.title: What owner Contains
docs.text:
The owner variable is a JSON object that may include:

  • Owner email address
  • API keys (public and private)
  • Subscription plan details
  • Purchase and expiry dates

This information is useful for admin features, billing checks, and integrations.

docs.title: Demo Owner Object
docs.text:
Example structure of the owner object (values masked):

{
  "mail": "owner@example.com",
  "api_keys": {
    "public": "pub-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx",
    "private": "sk-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx",
    "generated_at": "2025-11-07T16:33:19.208Z"
  },
  "plan": {
    "tier": "ELITE",
    "purchase_at": "2025-11-21T14:06:37.815Z",
    "expiry_at": "2026-08-18T12:01:06.657Z"
  }
}

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• owner is read-only
  • It exists only during command execution
  • API keys should never be shared or exposed to users

The owner variable is mainly intended for platform-level logic, not normal user-facing bot behavior.

docs.title: The params Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, params contains the extra text sent after a command.

It is useful when a command needs simple arguments or input.

docs.title: How params Works
docs.text:
If a user sends:

/start hello

Then:

  • Command → /start
  • Params → hello

So the value of params will be:

"hello"

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• params contains text only
  • It may be an empty string if no extra text is provided
  • It exists only during command execution

params is a simple way to pass arguments to commands without using reply-based input.

docs.title: The plan Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, plan contains subscription and feature details of the bot owner’s plan.

It tells you what limits and features are available for the current bot.

docs.title: What plan Is Used For
docs.text:
The plan variable helps you:

  • Check feature availability
  • Respect usage limits
  • Adjust behavior based on plan level

This is useful when building premium or restricted features.

docs.title: Demo Plan Object
docs.text:
Example structure of the plan object:

{
  "name": "Elite",
  "premium": true,
  "ads": false,
  "prop_limit": {
    "per_account": 100
  },
  "timeout": 60000,
  "buffer_size": 10485760,
  "parallel_process": 40,
  "support_contact": true,
  "sleep": 50
}

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• plan is read-only
  • It exists only during command execution
  • Values depend on the user’s active subscription

The plan variable allows bots to scale features safely based on account limits.

docs.title: The process Object
docs.text:
In TBL, process provides runtime information about the current execution environment.

It is mainly used to access environment variables that you configure from the bot dashboard.

docs.title: Accessing Environment Variables
docs.text:
Environment variables are available inside:

  • process.env

These values come directly from the bot’s Environment (ENV) settings in the dashboard.

For example, if you set an env key named API_KEY, you can access it using:

process.env.API_KEY

docs.title: Demo process Object
docs.text:
Example structure of the process object:

{
  "env": {
    "22": "Ok",
    "Test": "true",
    "Yest3": "Ok"
  },
  "pid": 652434,
  "MESSAGE": "For getting Env just use process.env.YOUR_ENV_NAME"
}

docs.title: What process Contains
docs.text:
Common properties include:

  • process.env → all configured environment variables
  • process.pid → current execution process ID
  • Additional runtime metadata

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• process is read-only
  • Environment values are always strings
  • Values exist only during command execution

The process object is the correct and safe way to store secrets, keys, and configuration for your bot.

docs.title: The request Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, request is a simplified version of update

TBL automatically detects the type of Telegram update and maps the relevant part into request.

docs.title: How request Works
docs.text:
For normal Telegram updates:

  • If the update type is message, then request is equal to update.message
  • If the update type is something else, request points to that specific part of the update

This means you don’t need to manually check update types in most cases.

Info

request helps you work with the useful data directly, without parsing the full update JSON.

docs.title: request in Webhook Mode
docs.text:
Info

ignore if you don't know abou Webhook feature in TBL.

When a command is triggered via webhook, request contains HTTP request data instead of Telegram message data.

It may include:

  • Request IP
  • Request body
  • URL parameters
  • Headers
  • Method and metadata

This makes request useful for building APIs, dashboards, and external integrations.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• request is read-only
  • It exists only during command execution
  • Its structure depends on how the command was triggered

For simple bots, you can use request instead of working with raw update.

docs.title: The tbl_options Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, tbl_options contains exactly what you pass to a callback command.

It is not wrapped or modified.

docs.title: How tbl_options Is Used
docs.text:
The tbl_options variable is used when:

  • A command is executed as a callback
  • A value is explicitly passed for the next command

It is not available in normal command execution.

docs.title: Example Value
docs.text:
If this value is passed:

{
  "key": "value"
}

Then tbl_options will be that exact value.

You can access it directly:

tbl_options.key

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• tbl_options exists only in callback commands
  • It can be any type (object, string, number, etc.)
  • If nothing is passed, it will be undefined

docs.title: The update Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, update is a JSON object that contains the Telegram update which triggered the command.

It is the raw data sent by Telegram for every interaction.

docs.title: What It Contains
docs.text:
The update JSON may include:

  • Message data
  • User information
  • Chat details
  • Update type information

The exact fields depend on what kind of update was received.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• update is read-only
  • It exists only during the current command execution
  • It represents the original Telegram payload

docs.title: Learn More
docs.text:
To understand the full structure of Telegram update JSON, see the official Telegram documentation:

core.telegram.org/bots/api#update

docs.title: The update_type Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, update_type is a string that tells you what kind of Telegram update triggered the command.

It helps you understand the context of the incoming update.

docs.title: Example Values
docs.text:
Some common values of update_type include:

  • message
  • chat_member
  • channel_post
  • poll
  • message_reaction
  • And more...

The value depends on the type of update received from Telegram.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• update_type is read-only
  • It exists only during command execution
  • It matches Telegram update type names

docs.title: Learn More
docs.text: For a full list of Telegram update types, see the Telegram Bot API Update object.

docs.title: The user Variable
docs.text:
In TBL, user contains information about the user interacting with the bot.

It represents the Telegram user related to the current update.

docs.title: What user Contains
docs.text: The user variable is a JSON object with details about the user.

docs.title: Demo User Object
docs.text:
Example structure of the user object:

{
  "id": 5723455420,
  "is_bot": false,
  "first_name": "Soumyadeep ∞",
  "username": "soumyadeepdas765",
  "language_code": "en",
  "is_premium": true,
  "last_name": "",
  "telegramid": 5723455420,
  "premium": true,
  "blocked": false,
  "block_reason": null,
  "blocked_at": null,
  "just_created": false
}

docs.title: When user Is Available
docs.text:
• If the update comes from a user interaction, user is an object
  • If the update does not involve a user, user can be null

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• user is either an object or null
  • It is read-only
  • It exists only during the current command execution

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
These pages answer the questions that come up once you've got a bot running but aren't sure which tool to reach for.

They sit between the tutorials (step-by-step walkthroughs) and the reference sections (method lists and variable docs). Read them when you're planning a feature, not when you're looking up a single method name.

docs.title: What's here
docs.text:
Bot vs Api — the most common early confusion. Both can send messages. This guide explains when each one actually makes sense, with real examples from bot projects.

More guides will land here over time — things like structuring multi-step flows, handling errors without scaring users, and when webhooks beat normal commands.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
If you haven't built a bot yet, start with Getting Started and Your First Bot.

If you know what you need and want the API details, jump straight to Api or Bot.

docs.title: Bot vs Api
docs.text: You'll see both Bot and Api in almost every TBL project. They overlap just enough to be confusing — both can send a message — but they're built for different jobs.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
Bot runs your bot. Api talks to Telegram.

When a user taps a button and you want to jump them into a checkout flow, that's Bot.runCommand(). When you need to edit the message they tapped, swap the inline keyboard, or answer a callback within Telegram's UI rules, that's Api.

docs.title: A concrete example
docs.text:
Imagine a /menu command that shows three options as inline buttons.

You could send the menu with either:

Bot.sendMessage("Pick one:", { reply_markup: "..." })

or

Api.sendMessage({
  text: "Pick one:",
  reply_markup: { inline_keyboard: [[{ text: "Help", callback_data: "help" }]] }
})

Both work for the initial send. The difference shows up next.

When the user taps Help, you get a callback update. To acknowledge it properly you call Api.answerCallbackQuery(). To replace the menu text in place, Api.editMessageText(). Bot doesn't wrap those — they're Telegram API territory.

If the tap should start a whole new conversation branch, you might do:

Api.answerCallbackQuery({ callback_query_id: update.callback_query.id })
Bot.runCommand("/help")

Bot for navigation. Api for the Telegram interaction around it.

docs.title: When Bot is the right call
docs.text:
Reach for Bot when you're orchestrating:

  • Running another command (Bot.runCommand)
  • Sending straightforward messages without touching Telegram's deeper options
  • Reading or writing bot-level storage
  • Listing users who've talked to your bot

Bot methods are shorter because TeleBotHost already knows the context. Less typing, fewer ways to pass a wrong chat_id.

docs.title: When Api is the right call
docs.text:
Reach for Api when Telegram's API is the product:

  • Inline keyboards and callback queries
  • Editing or deleting messages after they're sent
  • Reactions, pins, polls, stickers
  • Anything from the official method list that Bot doesn't wrap yet

Api gives you the full parameter set. That power comes with responsibility — you're closer to raw Telegram behavior, including its error codes.

docs.title: Case sensitivity
docs.text:
Both objects are case-sensitive. Bot.runCommand works. Bot.runcommand does not.

The msg instance has its own naming rules — check that page if you're mixing msg methods with Bot and Api in the same command.

docs.title: Still not sure?
docs.text:
Ask yourself: Am I changing what Telegram displays, or what my bot does internally?

Display → Api. Internal flow → Bot.

Many real commands use both in the same file. That's normal.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
Your bot lives on Telegram, but it doesn't have to stay there.

The HTTP instance sends requests to the outside world — your backend, a payment API, a weather service, anything with a URL. GET, POST, headers, JSON bodies: the usual fetch-style workflow, inside a command.

let res = await HTTP.get("https://api.example.com/status")

Use it when Telegram doesn't have the data you need, or when another system needs to know something happened in the bot.

docs.title: When HTTP fits
docs.text:
• Pulling live data (prices, scores, inventory) into a reply
  • POSTing form submissions to your server
  • Verifying a token against an auth API
  • Anything that isn't a Telegram method

For talking to Telegram, use Api. For talking out to the rest of the internet, use HTTP.

docs.title: Pages here
docs.text:
Page Covers Making Requests GET, POST, options, reading responses Fallback Commands Route success or failure to different commands

Responses from HTTP callbacks land in http_response and related globals when you use the fallback pattern.

docs.title: Using HTTP with Fallback Commands
docs.text:
TBL allows you to define success and error fallback commands when making HTTP requests.

These commands are executed automatically based on the result of the request.

If the error command is missing, the success command will run instead.

This makes HTTP workflows simple, safe, and predictable.

docs.title: Basic HTTP Request with Fallback Commands
docs.text:
You can attach success and error commands directly to an HTTP request.

Example: 

HTTP.get({
  url: "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1",
  success: "onSuccess",
  error: "onError",
  tbl_options: { key: value }
})

docs.title: tbl_options
docs.text:
• tbl_options is optional
  • Used to pass custom data to the next command
  • Available directly as tbl_options in the success or error command

Example access:

tbl_options.key

docs.title: How Command Execution Works
docs.text:
• If the HTTP request succeeds:
  • The success command is executed
  • options contains the HTTP response
  • If the HTTP request fails:
  • The error command is executed
  • options contains the HTTP error
  • If the error command is not defined:
  • The success command will be executed instead

Note

The error command runs only on real HTTP failures such as invalid URLs, network errors, or server errors (e.g. 500).

docs.title: Example Success Command
docs.text:
The success command receives HTTP response data.

Example: 

/*command: onSuccess*/
Bot.sendMessage("Fetched title: " + content)
On success, the following variables are available:

  • http_response
  • response
  • content (raw response body string)
  • headers
  • cookies

docs.title: Example Error Command
docs.text:
The error command receives HTTP error details.

Example: 

/*command: onError*/
Bot.sendMessage("HTTP request failed: " + error.status)
On error, the following are available:

  • error
  • options (error-related response data)
  • tbl_options (if provided)

docs.title: Available Response Data
docs.text:
On successful requests, detailed response information is available.

See full documentation here: HTTP Response

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
Tip

Use fallback commands to keep HTTP logic separate from message logic.

Warning

HTTP fallback commands do not catch TBL runtime errors. Those must be handled using the ! command.

This approach makes external API integration clean, modular, and easy to debug.

docs.title: Using the HTTP Instance
docs.text:
The HTTP instance allows your bot to make external API requests.

You can call any HTTP method using:

HTTP.method(...)

All common HTTP methods are supported, such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.

docs.title: Simple Request
docs.text:
The simplest form sends a request using only a URL.

Example: 

// Pass url as String 
HTTP.get("https://example.com")

docs.title: Using await to Get Response Data
docs.text:
To access the response data, use await.

Example: 

let res = await HTTP.get("https://example.com")
The returned value contains full information about the HTTP response.

Tip

Use await when you need to read the response body, status, or headers.

docs.title: Flexible Request Options
docs.text:
For more control, you can pass an options object.

Example: 

HTTP.get({
  url: "https://example.com",
  body: null,
  headers: {
    Authorization: "Bearer TOKEN"
  },
  params: {key: 1},
  timeout: 5000, //max 15s/15,000ms
  redirect: true,
  maxRedirect: 3
})

//Or 
HTTP.get("https://example.com", { options })

docs.title: Available Options
docs.text:
• url – Request URL
  • body – Request body (used in POST, PUT, etc.)
  • headers – Custom request headers
  • timeout – Request timeout in milliseconds
  • redirect – Enable or disable redirects
  • maxRedirect – Maximum redirect count (up to 3)

Note

Redirects are limited to avoid infinite loops.

docs.title: Demo HTTP Response
docs.text:
Example response object returned by an HTTP request:

{
  "ok": true,
  "status": 200,
  "statusText": "",
  "content": "OK",
  "data": "OK",
  "isJson": false,
  "headers": {
    "server": "nginx/1.24.0 (Ubuntu)",
    "date": "Mon, 22 Dec 2025 17:03:56 GMT",
    "content-type": "text/html; charset=utf-8",
    "content-length": "2",
    "connection": "keep-alive",
    "x-powered-by": "Express",
    "etag": "W/\"2-nOO9QiTIwXgNtWtBJezz8kv3SLc\""
  },
  "cookies": [],
  "url": "https://example.com",
  "redirected": false,
  "redirectCount": 0
}

docs.title: Understanding the Response
docs.text:
• ok – Whether the request succeeded
  • status – HTTP status code
  • content – Raw response body (string)
  • data – Parsed data (if JSON)
  • headers – Response headers
  • cookies – Cookies returned by the server

Info

When isJson is true, data contains the parsed JSON response.

docs.title: Learn More
docs.text: For a full breakdown of response fields, see : HTTP Response

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
Warning

External API failures do not crash your bot. Always check res.ok before using the response data.

The HTTP instance is best used for external integrations, data fetching, and service communication.

docs.title: TBL Libraries (Libs)
docs.text:
The Libs instance provides direct access to TBL's built-in helper libraries.

These libraries handle common bot tasks: randomization, date and time operations, resource tracking, referrals, and Telegram-specific utilities.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Libs.random.int(1, 100)
Libs.dateTimeFormat.now()
Libs.tgutil.getFullName(user)

Most methods return Promises. Using await is optional unless you need the returned value.

docs.title: What Libs Is Used For
docs.text:
Libs helps you avoid repetitive logic by offering ready-to-use helpers for:

  • Tracking counters, balances, and shared values
  • Formatting and calculating dates and times
  • Checking user membership in channels or groups
  • Generating random values
  • Building referral systems
  • Working with Telegram names, mentions, and formatting

docs.title: Available Libraries
docs.text: Library Description ResourcesLib User-level or global counters, balances, and persistent values dateTimeFormat Format dates, add or subtract time, calculate differences MCL Check channel or group membership random Generate random numbers, strings, colors, and dates refLib Create referral links and track invited users tgutil Telegram names, mentions, links, and text escaping

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Libs is available globally in TBL
  • No setup or imports are required
  • Designed for simplicity and performance
  • Works seamlessly with commands and callbacks

For general-purpose npm-style utilities, see Modules.

docs.title: dateTimeFormat
docs.text:
dateTimeFormat provides utilities for date and time formatting, calculations, and comparisons.

It is useful for working with timestamps, scheduling logic, and displaying dates in a human-readable format.

dateTimeFormat is available through the Libs instance.

docs.title: Get Current Date and Time
docs.text:
Get the current date/time using a custom format mask.

let now = Libs.dateTimeFormat.getCurrentDate(
  "yyyy-mm-dd HH:MM:ss"
)

This returns the current date formatted as a string.

docs.title: Add Days to a Date
docs.text:
You can add days to a given date.

let future = Libs.dateTimeFormat.addDays(
  new Date(),
  7
)

This returns a new date object representing a future date.

docs.title: Get Time Difference
docs.text:
Calculate the difference between two dates.

let diff = Libs.dateTimeFormat.getTimeDifference(
  "2025-01-01",
  "2025-02-01"
)

This returns the time difference between the two dates.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Supports custom date masks
  • Works with both strings and Date objects
  • Useful for scheduling, cooldowns, and expiration logic

docs.title: Full Documentation
docs.text: dateTimeFormat Documentation

docs.title: MCL (Membership Checker Lib)
docs.text:
MCL is used to validate whether a user is a member of one or more Telegram channels or groups.

It is commonly used to enforce join requirements before allowing users to access bot features.

MCL is available through the Libs instance.

docs.title: Check User Membership
docs.text:
You can check if a user has joined specific channels or groups.

let joined = await Libs.mcl.check(
  user.id,
  ["@Chan1", "@Chan2"]
)

This validates the user’s membership across all provided channels.

docs.title: Example Response
docs.text:
{
  all_joined: true,
  valid: ["@Channel1", "@Channel2"],
  left: [],
  invalid: [],
  details: [
    {
      channel: "@Channel1",
      member: { /* full getChatMember response */ }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Response Fields
docs.text:
• all_joined Indicates whether the user joined all required channels

  • valid Channels where the user is a valid member

  • left Channels the user has left or not joined

  • invalid Channels that are invalid or inaccessible

  • details Detailed membership data from Telegram

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Works with both channels and groups
  • Requires the bot to be present in the target chats
  • Useful for subscription-gated bots

docs.title: Full Documentation
docs.text: MCL Documentation

docs.title: random
docs.text:
The random library provides utilities for generating random values of different types.

It is useful for simulations, testing, games, unique identifiers, and dynamic content generation.

random is available through the Libs instance.

docs.title: Random Integer
docs.text:
Generate a random integer within a range.

let num = Libs.random.randomInt(1, 10)

This returns a number between 1 and 10.

docs.title: Random String
docs.text:
Generate a random string with custom length and character set.

let str = Libs.random.randomString(
  8,
  { charset: "alpha" }
)

This generates an 8-character alphabetic string.

docs.title: Random Date
docs.text:
Generate a random date within a given range.

let date = Libs.random.randomDate(
  new Date(2023, 0, 1),
  new Date(2025, 0, 1)
)

docs.title: Random Color
docs.text:
Generate a random color value.

let color = Libs.random.randomColor("rgb")

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Supports numbers, strings, dates, and colors
  • Useful for games, testing, and mock data
  • No setup required

docs.title: Full Documentation
docs.text: random Documentation

docs.title: refLib
docs.text:
refLib provides tools for creating and tracking referral systems.

It is useful for invite programs, growth tracking, and reward-based user onboarding.

refLib is available through the Libs instance.

docs.title: Create a Referral Link
docs.text:
Generate a referral link for the bot.

let refLink = Libs.refLib.getRefLink(bot.name)

This creates a unique referral link that can be shared with others.

docs.title: Count User Referrals
docs.text:
Get the number of users referred by a specific user.

let count = Libs.refLib.getRefCount(user.id)

This returns the total referral count for that user.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Referral tracking is handled automatically
  • Works across user sessions
  • Useful for reward or invite-based systems

docs.title: Full Documentation
docs.text: refLib Documentation

docs.title: ResourcesLib
docs.text:
ResourcesLib is used to manage persistent numeric resources at both user level and global level.

It is commonly used for things like balances, counters, credits, points, or usage tracking.

Resources created with ResourcesLib are stored persistently and automatically handled by TBL.

docs.title: User-Level Resources
docs.text:
User resources are scoped to the current user.

Example:

let coins = Libs.ResourcesLib.userRes("coins")

coins.add(50)
let current = coins.value()
  • Each user has their own independent value
  • Useful for coins, XP, credits, or limits

docs.title: Global Resources
docs.text:
Global resources are shared across all users of the same bot.

Any update to a global resource affects every user interacting with that bot.

Example:

let globalCounter = Libs.ResourcesLib.anotherRes("visits")

globalCounter.add(1)
  • One shared value for the entire bot
  • Useful for visits, totals, or bot-wide counters

Info

Global resources are bot-wide, not user-specific. They are not shared between different bots.

docs.title: Common Operations
docs.text:
Resources support simple operations such as:

  • Adding values
  • Reading current value
  • Persistent storage without manual save logic

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Resources are created automatically if they don’t exist
  • Values are stored persistently
  • No setup or schema required
  • Safe to use in commands and callbacks

docs.title: Full Documentation
docs.text: ResourcesLib Documentation

docs.title: tgutil
docs.text:
tgutil provides Telegram-specific helper utilities for working with users, text formatting, links, and buttons.

It helps simplify common Telegram-related tasks and ensures safe formatting across messages.

tgutil is available through the Libs instance.

docs.title: Get User’s Full Name
docs.text:
Combine first name and last name safely.

let fullName = Libs.tgutil.getFullName(user)

This returns a properly formatted full name for the user.

docs.title: Create a Clickable User Link
docs.text:
Generate a clickable link to a user profile.

let link = Libs.tgutil.getLinkFor(
  user,
  "html"
)

The format can be html or markdown.

docs.title: Escape Text Safely
docs.text:
Escape text to prevent formatting issues.

let safeText = Libs.tgutil.escapeText(
  "*Hello*",
  "markdown"
)

This ensures the text is safe to send in messages.

docs.title: Create an Inline Button
docs.text:
Generate an inline keyboard button.

let btn = Libs.tgutil.createInlineButton(
  "Press Me",
  "/callback_data"
)

The returned button can be used in reply_markup.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Useful for mentions, links, and formatting
  • Prevents Markdown and HTML injection issues
  • Designed for Telegram-specific workflows

docs.title: Full Documentation
docs.text: tgutil Documentation

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
The modules object provides access to preloaded utility libraries inside TBL.

It lets you perform common tasks — data processing, validation, formatting, and more — without importing or installing anything.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:

docs.title: bcrypt
docs.text:
bcrypt is used for secure password hashing and verification.

It is essential for safely storing passwords instead of saving them as plain text.

bcrypt functionality is available through the modules object.

docs.title: Hashing a Password
docs.text:
const hash = await modules.bcrypt.hash(
  "password123",
  10
)
  • The second argument is the salt rounds
  • Higher values increase security but take more time

docs.title: Verifying a Password
docs.text:
const match = await modules.bcrypt.compare(
  "password123",
  hash
)

This checks whether the password matches the stored hash.

docs.title: Example Output
docs.text:
hash  → "$2b$10$e0N...."
match → true

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Always store hashes, never raw passwords
  • Use a reasonable salt round value (e.g. 10–12)
  • Comparison is safe against timing attacks

docs.title: crypto
docs.text:
The crypto utility provides cryptographic functions such as hashing, encryption, and decryption.

It is useful for:

docs.text:
const hash = crypto
  .createHash("sha256")
  .update("data")
  .digest("hex")

  .createHash("sha256")
  .update("data")
  .digest("hex")

docs.title: msg Instance
docs.text:
The msg instance is used to interact with Telegram messages through methods like msg.replyText(), msg.editText(), and msg.delete().

Not the same as the global msg variable

This page documents the msg instance (message methods). For the read-only global msg variable, see msg (global).

It allows you to perform message-level actions such as:

  • Send messages
  • Reply to messages
  • Edit messages
  • Delete messages
  • Forward or copy messages
  • Add reactions
  • Perform chat actions (like typing, upload, etc.)

All msg methods return Promises.

Using await is optional — it is required only when you need access to the response object for further actions.

The msg instance works only when a message context exists, meaning it is available in message-based updates.

docs.title: msg as an Object
docs.text:
The msg instance also acts as a message object.

It contains the full Telegram message data for the current update.

docs.title: Common Properties
docs.text:
• msg.text Message text (if any)

  • msg.chat Chat information (id, type, title, etc.)

  • msg.from Sender information

  • msg.message_id Unique message identifier

  • msg.date Message timestamp

All standard Telegram Message fields are available through msg.

docs.title: Availability
docs.text:
• The msg object exists only for message-based updates
  • It is not available for non-message updates (like callbacks or webhooks)
  • All message-related actions rely on this object

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• All msg methods are case-insensitive Example: msg.replyPhoto() and msg.replyphoto() both work

  • Markdown parsing is enabled by default for text replies

  • msg provides both data access and action methods in one place

docs.title: Using the msg Instance
docs.text:
The msg instance is used to interact with the current Telegram message.

It allows replying, sending new messages, editing, deleting, reacting, forwarding, and performing chat actions.

All msg methods return Promises. Using await is optional and only needed if you want the response object.

docs.title: Available Methods
docs.text:
• Core Messaging msg.reply() msg.send()

  • Media Messages msg.replyPhoto() msg.replyVideo() msg.replyDocument()

  • Message Management msg.editText() msg.delete() msg.react() msg.pin() msg.unpin()

  • Forwarding & Copying msg.forward() msg.copy()

  • Special Messages msg.replySticker() msg.replyDice()

  • Chat Actions msg.sendChatAction()

docs.title: Core Messaging
docs.text:
Reply to the current message:

msg.reply("Hello!")
let result = await msg.reply("Hello!")

Send a new message:

msg.send("This is a new message")
await msg.send("This is a new message", { parse_mode: "Markdown" })

docs.title: Media Messages
docs.text:
Reply with a photo:

msg.replyPhoto("https://example.com/cat.jpg", { caption: "Cute cat 🐱" })
await msg.replyPhoto("https://example.com/cat.jpg", { caption: "Cute cat 🐱" })

Reply with a video:

msg.replyVideo("https://example.com/video.mp4")
await msg.replyVideo("https://example.com/video.mp4", { caption: "Watch this!" })

Reply with a document:

msg.replyDocument("file.pdf")
await msg.replyDocument("file.pdf")

docs.title: Message Management
docs.text:
Edit message text:

msg.editText("Updated text")
await msg.editText("Updated text", { parse_mode: "Markdown" })

Delete a message:

msg.delete(msg.message_id)
await msg.delete(msg.message_id)

React to a message:

msg.react("👍")
msg.react("🔥", true)

Pin and unpin messages:

msg.pin()
msg.unpin(msg.message_id)

docs.title: Forwarding & Copying
docs.text:
Forward a message:

msg.forward(123456789)
await msg.forward(123456789)

Copy a message:

msg.copy(123456789, { caption: "Copied message" })
await msg.copy(123456789, { caption: "Copied message" })

docs.title: Special Messages
docs.text:
Reply with a sticker:

msg.replySticker("CAACAgUAAxkBAAECX-9g1...")
await msg.replySticker("CAACAgUAAxkBAAECX-9g1...")

Reply with a dice:

msg.replyDice("🎲")
await msg.replyDice("🎲")

docs.title: Chat Actions
docs.text:
Show typing indicator:

msg.sendChatAction("typing")
await msg.sendChatAction("typing")

Other supported actions include:

  • upload_photo
  • record_video
  • record_audio
  • upload_document

docs.title: Chained Methods
docs.text:
When you use await, msg methods support chained actions.

let data = await msg.reply("Hello!")
data.pin()

More details about chained methods: Api chained

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Work through these in order if you're new to TBL. Each one builds on the last — by the end you'll have a bot that handles commands, buttons, aliases, typed input, and unknown messages.

You don't need to write much code at first. TeleBotHost lets you get a working bot using only the command editor. Logic comes later, when you need it.

docs.title: The series
docs.text:
1. Command Structure — how TBL thinks about triggers, answers, logic, and the special commands (@, !, *, and the rest). Read this before touching anything else.
  2. Your First Bot — a /start command that actually replies. Takes about five minutes.
  3. Adding a Keyboard — replace typing with tap-able buttons.
  4. Using Aliases — one command, several ways to trigger it.
  5. Handling User Input — wait for the user's next message and use it.
  6. Wildcard Command — catch everything that doesn't match anything else.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: Make sure you've added a bot on TeleBotHost and launched it at least once. The tutorials assume you can open the Commands panel and see your bot respond on Telegram.

docs.title: User Instance
docs.text:
The User instance is used to store and manage data at the user level.

Just like the Bot instance stores data for the bot, the User instance stores data separately for each user.

Each user has their own private storage, and data saved for one user is not shared with others.

This is useful for:

  • User preferences
  • User-specific settings
  • Progress or flow state
  • Any per-user information

User-level data is automatically scoped to the current user, so you don’t need to manage user IDs manually.

docs.title: Advanced User Instance Usage
docs.text:
This section covers advanced User instance usage.

It includes object-based operations and working with user data beyond simple string-based calls.

docs.title: Object-Based Operations
docs.text:
In addition to string-based methods, the User instance supports object-style usage.

This allows passing extra options when needed.

docs.title: Setting Data with Object Format
docs.text:
User.set({
  key: "score",
  value: 100
})

This behaves the same as string-based User.set, but allows more flexibility.

docs.title: Working with a Specific User
docs.text:
You can explicitly target a specific user by passing user_id.

This is useful for admin tools or background logic.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
User.set({
  key: "status",
  value: "verified",
  user_id: 123456789
})

If user_id is not provided, the current user is used automatically.

docs.title: Reading Data for a Specific User
docs.text:
let status = User.get({
  key: "status",
  user_id: 123456789
})

This reads data from the specified user instead of the current one.

docs.title: Deleting Data for a Specific User
docs.text:
User.del({
  key: "status",
  user_id: 123456789
})

Only the targeted user’s data is affected.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Object format is optional
  • Useful for advanced flows and admin logic
  • All data remains isolated per user
  • User-level storage is independent from Bot-level storage
  • Use this carefully to avoid unintended changes to other users

docs.title: Basic User Operations
docs.text:
Use the User instance to store and read data at the user level.

All operations here use the string-based method format and apply only to the current user.

docs.title: Saving User Data
docs.text:
Use User.set() to store values.

User.set("name", "Alice")
User.set("age", 25, "number")
  • First argument: key
  • Second argument: value
  • Third argument (optional): data type

If the type is not provided, TBL will auto-detect it.

docs.title: Reading User Data
docs.text:
Use User.get() to read stored values.

let name = User.get("name")
let age = User.get("age")

Bot.sendMessage("Name: " + name + ", Age: " + age)

Reading data is synchronous and returns the value directly.

If a key does not exist, it returns null.

docs.title: Deleting a Single Value
docs.text:
Remove a specific value when it’s no longer needed.

User.del("age")

let age = User.get("age")   // null
Bot.sendMessage("After delete, age = " + age)

Deleting a non-existing key does nothing and does not throw an error.

docs.title: Bulk Operations
docs.text:
Bulk operations let you work with all stored user data at once.

These are useful when you want to inspect or reset the user’s data.

docs.title: Get All User Data
docs.text:
let all = User.getAll()
Bot.inspect(all)

Example output:

{
  "name": "Alice",
  "age": 25
}

This returns an object containing all stored keys and values for the user.

docs.title: Delete All User Data
docs.text:
User.delAll()

let all2 = User.getAll()
Bot.inspect(all2)

This clears all data for the current user.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• All data is stored at the user level
  • Data is private and isolated per user
  • Only string-based methods are used here
  • Reading (get, getAll) is synchronous
  • Saving and deleting do not require await
  • Missing keys always return null

docs.title: Webapp Instance
docs.text:
The Webapp instance is used to generate clean and global URLs for your bot web integrations, such as dashboards, pages, and lightweight APIs.

Unlike Webhook, Webapp URLs are not cryptographically signed, so they are ideal for public or embed-style resources.

Public URL Behavior

Webapp URLs are public and do not contain user authentication data. Use them for pages that do not require secure user verification.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use the Webapp class when you need static or semi-dynamic links for:

  • Landing pages or info dashboards
  • Public web components or previews
  • Lightweight APIs or micro webviews
  • Embedded pages that do not require signed user context

Security Note

Webapp URLs are public and are not signed. For sensitive or user-specific actions, use Webhook URLs.

docs.title: Webapp Best Practices
docs.text:
Follow these practices when building public webapp endpoints:

  • Use Webapp only for public or semi-public resources.
  • Use params for readable URL parameters (example: ?ref=home&lang=en).
  • Use options for app-level configuration.
  • Keep sensitive values out of URL query strings.
  • For secure or user-specific links, use Webhook.

Security Reminder

Webapp URLs are public and are not cryptographically signed. Use Webhook for any sensitive or authenticated flow.

docs.title: JSON API Endpoint (User-Based Webhook)
docs.text:
This example returns structured JSON for a user-based webhook where the user object is available:

let userData = {
  id: user.id,
  name: user.first_name,
  premium: user.premium || false,
  join_date: user.join_date
}

res.status(200)
   .set("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", "*")
   .json({
     status: "success",
     data: userData,
     timestamp: Date.now()
   })

Note

The user object is available in user-based webhooks only. Public Webapp URLs do not include authenticated user context — use static or query-parameter data instead.

docs.title: Simple Public Dashboard Link
docs.text:
Generate a public Webapp URL and send it in a Telegram message:

let publicDashboard = Webapp.getUrl("dashboard", {
  params: { ref: "docs", lang: "en" }
})

Api.sendMessage({
  text: `Open dashboard: ${publicDashboard}`
})

docs.title: Template Rendering with res.render()
docs.text:
This page covers how res.render() passes data into rendered commands and templates.

For the complete method reference and practical examples, see the res.render() Guide.

docs.title: Automatic Content Type Detection
docs.text:
res.render() sets the correct Content-Type from the file extension:

res.render("page.html")   // text/html
res.render("data.json")   // application/json
res.render("script.js")   // application/javascript
res.render("style.css")   // text/css
res.render("api.xml")     // application/xml
res.render("plain-text")  // text/plain

docs.title: Data Passing and Template Context
docs.text:
Pass data using the second argument:

// Webapp URL: /webapp/showProfile?section=settings&view=compact

res.render("profile-template.html", {
  data: {
    user: user,
    profile: userProfile,
    preferences: userPrefs
  }
})

Inside the rendered template you can access:

  • Custom fields from data (e.g. profile, preferences)
  • params — URL query parameters ({ section: "settings", view: "compact" })
  • Global TBL variables (Api, Bot, msg, request, etc.)
  • user — only in user-based webhooks, not in public Webapp URLs

Warning

Webapp URLs are public and unsigned. Do not expose sensitive user data through public Webapp endpoints.

docs.text: Method Purpose set(key, value) Set HTTP response headers status(code) Set HTTP status code send(body) Send any content type (auto-detected) json(obj) Send JSON with application/json html(content) Send HTML (EJS auto-rendered if detected) xml(content) Send XML with application/xml text(content) Send plain text (EJS auto-rendered if detected) redirect(url) Redirect to a URL or command render(path, options) Render another command as the response

// HTML page
res.html("<h1>Welcome</h1>")

// Redirect
res.redirect("https://example.com/done")

// Render a template command
res.render("dashboard.html", { data: { stats: statsData } })

docs.title: getUrl(command, { options, params })
docs.text:
Generates a global webapp URL for the specified command.

  • Use options for internal configuration.
  • Use params for visible query parameters.
let dashboardUrl = Webapp.getUrl("dashboard", {
  options: { theme: "dark", userId: 123 },
  params: { ref: "home", lang: "en" }
})

Api.sendMessage({
  text: `Open the web dashboard: ${dashboardUrl}`
})

docs.title: URL Design Tips
docs.text:
• Keep command names clear and predictable.
  • Put internal app config in options.
  • Put readable query values in params.
  • Avoid passing sensitive data in URL params.

docs.title: Webhook Instance
docs.text:
The Webhook instance is used to generate secure webhook URLs for your bot.

These URLs allow external sources—such as websites, APIs, or dashboards—to trigger bot commands directly.

Each webhook URL is protected using cryptographic signatures, ensuring that only valid and authorized requests can execute commands.

This is useful when you want:

  • Website → bot interactions
  • API-driven bot actions
  • Secure external triggers
  • Automation without exposing bot tokens

Webhook-triggered commands behave like normal TBL commands, but are executed through a secure HTTP endpoint.

docs.title: Global Webhooks
docs.text:
Global webhooks execute commands without any user context.

They are designed for system-level or public actions where no specific user or chat is involved.

In global webhooks:

  • user is null
  • chat is null
  • The command runs at the account level

These are ideal for dashboards, public pages, cron jobs, or backend services.

docs.title: getGlobalUrl(command, { options, params, redirect })
docs.text:
Creates a globally accessible webhook URL.

This URL does not require user authentication and can be triggered by any external source.

  • command → command to execute
  • options → custom data passed to the command
  • params → extra query parameters
  • redirect → optional URL to redirect after execution

Example:

let statsUrl = Webhook.getGlobalUrl("getStats", {
  options: { days: 30 },
  redirect: "https://telebothost.com",
  params: { ref: "home" }
})

Api.sendMessage({
  text: `View global statistics: ${statsUrl}`
})

docs.title: How Global Webhooks Behave
docs.text:
• Commands run without user or chat data
  • Useful for account-wide logic
  • Suitable for read-only or system actions
  • Safe for public or automated triggers

Warning

Since global webhooks have no user context, avoid using them for actions that modify user data.

docs.title: Execution & Response
docs.text:
• Global webhook execution returns a 2xx HTTP response by default
  • Redirects are handled automatically if redirect is provided
  • You can manually control responses using the res instance

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Global webhooks are secure and signed
  • Parameters and options are protected
  • Best used for dashboards, analytics, and automation

docs.title: Handling Webhooks
docs.text:
Handling webhooks in TBL is very easy.

When a command is triggered via a webhook, you automatically get access to the request object.

This object contains all details about the incoming HTTP request.

docs.title: Accessing the request Object
docs.text:
Inside a webhook-triggered command, you can read request.

Example structure:

{
  "url": "/ownlang/webhook/5484560?command=data&options=%7B%22level%22%3A10%7D&sig=...",
  "method": "GET",
  "headers": {
    "host": "prod-api.telebothost.com",
    "user-agent": "Reqable/2.33.12",
    "x-real-ip": "157.34.201.36"
  },
  "ip": "157.34.201.36",
  "query": {
    "command": "data",
    "options": "{\"level\":10}",
    "sig": "SECURE_SIGNATURE",
    "user": "5723455420",
    "ref": "profile",
    "lang": "en"
  },
  "body": null
}

This gives you full control over query parameters, headers, IP address, and request method.

docs.title: Difference from Telegram Updates
docs.text:
• For Telegram updates, data is available under update.{type}
  • For webhook execution, data comes from the request object

This makes webhook handling closer to normal HTTP request handling.

docs.title: Message Sending in Webhooks
docs.text:
All other TBL features work the same inside webhook commands.

However, there is one important difference:

Warning

In global webhooks, there is no user or chat context.

Because of this:

  • Bot message helpers may not work automatically
  • When using Api.xxx, you must pass chat_id explicitly

User-based webhooks do not have this limitation.

docs.title: Security & Restrictions
docs.text:
Some features may be restricted or limited in webhook commands.

This is intentional and helps:

  • Prevent abuse
  • Protect system resources
  • Keep webhook execution safe

Note

Webhooks are signed and verified automatically. Invalid or modified requests will not execute.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Webhook commands receive a request object
  • Query parameters and headers are fully accessible
  • Telegram updates use update, webhooks use request
  • Global webhooks require explicit chat_id for sending messages
  • Some features may be disabled for safety

docs.title: Sending Custom HTTP Responses
docs.text:
In webhook and Webapp commands, you can send a custom HTTP response back to the caller using the built-in res instance.

This is useful when:

  • Building APIs with TBL
  • Returning JSON to external services
  • Acknowledging webhook calls manually
  • Serving HTML or redirect responses

docs.title: Using the res Instance
docs.text:
Send a JSON response like this:

res.json({ ok: true })

This immediately sends a response to the caller and ends execution.

You can return any valid JSON object depending on your use case.

Tip

Use res.json() when your endpoint acts like an API and the caller expects structured data.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The res instance is available in webhook commands and Webapp commands
  • Once a response is sent, no further output is processed
  • If no custom response is sent, a default 2xx response is returned

docs.title: Full Reference
docs.text:
For all response methods (json, html, render, redirect, and more), see the Response (res) overview.

For advanced template rendering, see the res.render() Guide.

docs.title: User-Based Webhooks
docs.text:
User-based webhooks execute commands in the context of a user. This means user and chat are available inside the command.

They are useful for triggering bot actions from websites, dashboards, or external APIs on behalf of a user.

docs.title: getUrl(command, { options, params, redirect })
docs.text:
Generates a secure webhook URL for the current user.

  • command → command to execute
  • options → custom data passed to the command
  • params → extra query parameters
  • redirect → optional URL to redirect after execution

Example:

let syncUrl = Webhook.getUrl("syncGameData", {
  options: { level: 10 },
  params: { ref: "profile", lang: "en" }
})

Api.sendMessage({
  text: `Sync your game data: ${syncUrl}`
})

docs.title: Generate Webhook for a Specific User
getUrlFor({ user_id, command, options, params, redirect })
docs.text:
Generates a personalized webhook URL for a specific user ID.

This is ideal for sending links that should work only for a given user.

Example:

let upgradeUrl = Webhook.getUrlFor({
  user_id: 123,
  command: "syncGameData",
  redirect: "https://telebothost.com",
  options: { plan: "pro" },
  params: { ref: "upgrade" }
})

Api.sendMessage({
  text: `Upgrade your plan here: ${upgradeUrl}`
})

docs.title: Example Webhook URL
docs.text:
A generated webhook URL may look like this:

https://prod-api.telebothost.com/ownlang/webhook/XXXXXXX
?command=syncGameData
&options=%7B%22level%22%3A10%7D
&sig=SECURE_SIGNATURE
&user=USER_ID
&ref=profile
&lang=en

Values are signed and protected. Changing them will invalidate the request.

docs.title: Execution & Response
docs.text:
• By default, webhook execution returns a 2xx HTTP response
  • This indicates successful command execution
  • Redirects are handled automatically when redirect is provided

Note

You can also use the res instance to control the HTTP response manually.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• User-based webhooks always include user context
  • user and chat are available in the command
  • Options and params are safely signed
  • URLs cannot be forged or reused for other users
  • Ideal for user-specific actions and flows

docs.title: Webhook Types
docs.text: The Webhook instance supports two types of webhook execution, depending on how the webhook is created and used.

docs.title: User-Based Webhook
docs.text:
A user-based webhook executes a command in the context of a specific user.

In this type:

  • user is available
  • chat is available
  • The command behaves like a normal user-triggered command

This is useful when:

  • A web action should act on behalf of a user
  • You need access to user-specific or chat-specific data
  • The webhook is linked to a logged-in user or session

User-based webhooks allow full interaction with user and chat data.

docs.title: Global Webhook
docs.text:
A global webhook is not tied to any user.

In this type:

  • user is null
  • chat is null
  • The command runs at a global level

This is useful when:

  • The webhook is triggered by a system or service
  • No user context is required
  • You want to perform background or account-level actions

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Both webhook types are secure and signed
  • Both trigger normal TBL commands
  • The difference is only the availability of user and chat
